quote: a supremacy that past ages cannot match and future ages will not surpass.
problem: ἀνυπόστατον μὲν τοῖς ὑπάρχουσι πᾶσιν, ἀνυπέρβλητον δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἐπιγινομένοις: τοῖς ὑπάρχουσι = all those now existing (present), not past ages; ἀνυπόστατον = irresistible (cannot be withstood), not 'cannot match'. Temporal sense shifted from present to past.
proposed_fix: a supremacy that no one now living can resist and that no one in future ages can surpass.

quote: For it is no more likely that the one will ever properly arrange treatments for the body than that the man of affairs will be able to handle any situation that arises as he should, without knowledge of the things just mentioned.
problem: Greek is a double negative correlative, οὔτε γὰρ ἐκεῖνον εἰκὸς οὐδέποτε δεόντως συστήσασθαι ... οὔτε τὸν πραγματικὸν οὐδὲν οἷόν τε κατὰ τρόπον χειρίσαι: it says both are impossible ('neither ... nor'). 'No more likely ... than' turns this into a comparison and asserts neither impossibility.
proposed_fix: For neither is it likely that the one will ever properly arrange treatments for the body, nor is it possible for the man of affairs to handle any situation that arises as he should, without knowledge of the things just mentioned.

quote: he would at once have sought another pretext and begun preparations for action
problem: Greek εὐθέως ἂν ἄλλην ἀρχὴν ἐποιεῖτο καὶ παρασκευὴν πραγμάτων: 'he would at once have made another beginning', i.e. started another war. The word is ἀρχή, not πρόφασις, and Polybius has just spent chs. 6-7 keeping the two apart. 'Pretext' substitutes the very term he is contrasting it with.
proposed_fix: he would at once have made a fresh beginning and begun preparations for action

quote: because they take their initial premises to be false and irrational
problem: διὰ τὸ τὰς πρώτας ὑποθέσεις ψευδεῖς καὶ παραλόγους λαμβάνειν = because they adopt initial premises that are false and irrational. The English says the playwrights regard their premises as false, which is not the sense: they adopt false premises without knowing it.
proposed_fix: because the initial premises they adopt are false and irrational

quote: to join in helping him secure the throne, he agreed,
problem: The Greek has a lacuna marked *** between συμπεριποιῆσαι τὴν ἀρχὴν αὐτῷ and ὑπήκουσε; the English reads straight on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: to join in helping him secure the throne, [...] he agreed,

quote: and attacked, [seizing] a certain gorge that was hard to pass and ringed with cliffs [...]
problem: There is no lacuna. The Greek sentence carries across the chapter break: ἐπιτίθενται, φάραγγά τινα δύσβατον καὶ κρημνώδη | (53.1) περαιουμένων αὐτῶν, 'they attack them while they were crossing a certain gorge, hard to pass and precipitous'. The accusative φάραγγα is the object of περαιουμένων. Nothing in the Greek means 'seizing'; the bracketed verb is made up to fill a gap that is not there. Chapter 53 already renders περαιουμένων ('While they were crossing'), so chapter 52 only needs the attack and the place.
proposed_fix: and attacked them in a certain gorge that was hard to pass and ringed with cliffs [...]

quote: The Romans now had to carry on the fight over the bodies of the fallen.
problem: The opening πεπτωκότας ἐποιοῦντο τὴν μάχην is the end of the sentence split across the chapter boundary: στρεφόμενοι πρὸς τοὺς ἐκ τῶν πλαγίων προσ|πεπτωκότας ἐποιοῦντο τὴν μάχην, 'turning against those who had fallen upon them from the flanks, they kept up the fight'. πεπτωκότας is the second half of προσπεπτωκότας (the attackers), not 'the fallen' (the dead). The English makes up a scene of fighting over corpses that the Greek does not contain.
proposed_fix: [...] kept up the fight.

quote: and one may grasp the magnitude of that change from what follows.
problem: Greek: γνοίη δ᾽ ἄν τις τὸ μέγεθος τῆς μεταβολῆς ἐκ τούτων. ζήτει ἐν τῷ περὶ στρατηγίας. The excerptor's note ('look in the section on generalship') shows the excerpt breaks off here: the passage that 'follows' (ἐκ τούτων) is not transmitted. The English reads straight on into an unrelated fragment as if the promised illustration came next.
proposed_fix: and one may grasp the magnitude of that change from what follows. [...]

quote: they came to think that their rulers ought to have distinctive clothing
problem: ὑπέλαβον δεῖν ἔχειν τοὺς ἡγουμένους τῶν ὑποταττομένων ἐξάλλους ἐσθῆτας: the hereditary kings themselves think that rulers should have dress distinct from (genitive of comparison) that of the subjects. 'their rulers' makes the kings' rulers the object and drops the contrast with the subjects.
proposed_fix: they came to think that rulers ought to have clothing distinct from that of their subjects

quote: [...] and for thirty years after that period, was continually being refined
problem: Greek: '**** καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτεσιν ὕστερον ἀπὸ τούτων τῶν καιρῶν ἀεὶ ... προδιευκρινουμένων ἦν' = '[...] and thirty years later; from those times on it was continually being refined'. ἔτεσιν ὕστερον means 'years later' (a point in time), not 'for thirty years' (a duration), and ἀπὸ τούτων τῶν καιρῶν begins the refinement. 'καὶ τριάκοντα' may be the tail of a compound numeral lost in the lacuna, so 'thirty' may not be the whole figure.
proposed_fix: [...] and thirty years later; from that time on it was continually being refined

quote: within the forty-six years counted from his coming of age
problem: ἐν τοῖς τετταράκοντα καὶ ἓξ ἔτεσιν ἀπὸ γενεᾶς = within the forty-six years from birth, i.e. before the age of forty-six; 'from his coming of age' shifts the age limit by some seventeen years.
proposed_fix: before reaching the age of forty-six

quote: ten thousand drachmas (asses)
problem: ὑπὲρ τὰς μυρίας τιμώμενοι δραχμάς = rated above 10,000 drachmas. The gloss '(asses)' equates drachmas with asses; Polybius's drachma = denarius, so the figure corresponds to 100,000 asses (first census class), not 10,000.
proposed_fix: ten thousand drachmas

quote: place the market-place, quartermaster’s office, and headquarters between the two camps
problem: μέσον τιθέασι τῶν δυεῖν στρατοπέδων: here στρατόπεδον means legion, as everywhere in this section (εἰς ἕκαστον στρατόπεδον = 'each legion', translated so in this same chapter). A consul camping on his own with his two legions puts the forum, quaestorium and praetorium between those two legions, not 'between the two camps', which would wrongly suggest the two consuls' separate camps.
proposed_fix: place the market-place, quartermaster’s office, and headquarters between the two legions

quote: the duty falls to each maniple only once every four days
problem: παρὰ τετάρτην ἡμέραν counts inclusively: 'every third day'. That agrees with the arithmetic, since three maniples take turns (ἀνὰ μέρος) serving each tribune, so each serves one day in three. 'Once every four days' is wrong by one.
proposed_fix: the duty falls to each maniple only every third day

quote: and most of them are killed on the spot inside the camp itself
problem: τοὺς μὲν πλείστους ... καταβάλλουσι, τοῖς δ᾽ ἐκπεσεῖν δυναμένοις: the μέν/δέ pair contrasts the condemned men who are killed with those who escape. In the English, 'them' refers grammatically back to 'all the men in the camp', which makes the attackers the ones killed.
proposed_fix: and most of those condemned are killed on the spot inside the camp itself

quote: Hannibal could say nothing against the daring and practical force of the proposal
problem: The Greek marks a gap after Monomachus' proposal (συνήθεις. ... Ἀννίβας δὲ πρὸς μὲν τὸ τόλμημα); the English runs straight on as if continuous.
proposed_fix: [...] Hannibal could say nothing against the daring and practical force of the proposal

quote: these men had divided their operations between themselves in a very grand fashion, and although
problem: γενναιότατα κεκοινωνηκότας ἑαυτοῖς πραγμάτων = 'had been partners with each other in affairs most loyally'. κοινωνέω means to share or be partners, not to divide. 'Divided' cancels the contrast the Greek draws: they had been partners since youth, yet they never took part in the same operation.
proposed_fix: these men had been partners in affairs with each other most loyally, and although

quote: And I heard it even more precisely from Masannasus, who
problem: The Greek has a gap marker after Μασαννάσου (Μασαννάσου... ἀκριβέστερον διήκουσα); the English reads on as though the text were whole. The sense still holds, so this may be a minor gap only.
proposed_fix: And I heard it even more precisely from Masannasus [...], who

quote: he was in his eighteenth year
problem: Greek ἑπτακαιδέκατον ἔτος ἔχων = 'in his seventeenth year'; the English number is off by one.
proposed_fix: he was in his seventeenth year

quote: instead devised and proposed actions that the enemy themselves did not anticipate.
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: τὰ δὲ μήτε παρὰ τοῖς πολεμίοις *, ταῦτ᾽ ἐπενόει. The μήτε correlative ('neither among the enemy ... nor ...') is cut off by the gap. The English smooths over it, inventing 'did not anticipate' and dropping the 'neither' construction.
proposed_fix: instead devised and proposed actions that neither among the enemy … [the Greek text has a gap here] …

quote: Opposite it on the west is another hill in a corresponding position
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: τούτῳ δ᾽ ὁ * ἀπὸ τῆς δύσεως ἀντίκειται. A word (probably the hill's name or a qualifier) has dropped out after ὁ; the English supplies 'another hill' and reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: Opposite it on the west is the [...] hill, in a corresponding position

quote: —yet this is only one part, as it seems to me, of practical history.
problem: Greek has a lacuna: προσφέρεσθαι, *** μέρος, ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, πρὸς τὴν πραγματικὴν ἱστορίαν. The words 'yet this is only one' are supplied with no gap marked; only μέρος survives.
proposed_fix: —[...] part, as it seems to me, of practical history.

quote: which was straightforward and fought with the army in a single body
problem: καθ᾽ ἕν τι μέρος τῆς δυνάμεως means 'with only one part of the forces' (the battle was decided by a single division). The English says the opposite, that the whole army fought as one body.
proposed_fix: which was straightforward and involved only one part of the forces

quote: he says they had fixed their attention and learned how great a difference war makes from peace
problem: λοιπόν φησιν αὐτοὺς ἐπιστήσαντας μαθεῖν ἡλίκην ὁ πόλεμος διαφορὰν ἔχει τῆς εἰρήνης: φησί + infinitive here is an exhortation, 'he tells them they must now attend and learn' how great the difference is. That is the absurdity Polybius points out: Hermocrates tells men he has just praised for knowing the difference that they must learn it. The current English makes it a statement of fact that they had already learned it, which takes the point away.
proposed_fix: he tells them that they must now give their attention and learn how great a difference war makes from peace

quote: [he leaves none of them...] [...] [the text breaks off]
problem: The Greek breaks off at οὐδένα τῶν ('none of the ...'). It has no verb, so 'he leaves' is supplied text; the bracket presents a conjecture as if it were a gloss on the Greek.
proposed_fix: none of the [...] [the text breaks off]

quote: and at last, though fortune had already given them warning, had advanced so far
problem: Greek τὸ δὲ τέλος ὑπὸ τῆς τύχης οὔπω νουθετούμενοι = 'at last, not yet admonished by Fortune' (οὔπω negates); the English inverts it to 'though fortune had already given them warning'.
proposed_fix: and at last, still not taught a lesson by Fortune, had advanced so far

quote: For his own part, he said, experience had taught him that
problem: Greek ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν ἕτοιμός εἰμι τῷ πεῖραν εἰληφέναι = 'I for my part am ready [for this], because I have learned by experience'; ἕτοιμός εἰμι is dropped, which removes the 'I am ready' half of the ἐγὼ μὲν … σὲ δ᾽ contrast that continues in ch. 7.
proposed_fix: For his own part, he said, he was ready to do this, because experience had taught him that

quote: Should he, Scipio said, put himself in Hannibal’s place and remove the harshest of the imposed terms,
problem: Greek σὺ τὴν ἐμὴν χώραν μεταλαβὼν εἶπον = 'you (Hannibal), taking my place, tell me': Scipio asks Hannibal to put himself in Scipio's place. The English reverses the persons.
proposed_fix: Let Hannibal, Scipio said, put himself in Scipio’s place and say: should the Romans remove the harshest of the imposed terms,

quote: once they go into battle with no hope left except in fighting.
problem: Greek ἐπειδὰν ἀπελπίσαντες τοῦ ζῆν ἴωσιν εἰς τὴν μάχην = 'when they go into battle having despaired of life'; the hope abandoned is of survival, not 'hope except in fighting'.
proposed_fix: once they go into battle having given up all hope of life.

quote: and by this Masinissa quickly stripped the Carthaginian left wing of its mounted support.
problem: Greek has a lacuna: Νομάδων: *** τῶν περὶ τὸν Μασαννάσαν ταχέως ἐψιλώθη τὸ λαιὸν κέρας τῶν Καρχηδονίων. The link between the elephants' stampede and Masinissa's action is lost; 'by this' is invented, and the surviving clause is passive ('the left wing was quickly laid bare'), with Masinissa's men in a genitive whose construction is lost.
proposed_fix: [a gap in the text] … of Masinissa's men, the Carthaginian left wing was quickly stripped of its cavalry.

quote: against Romans armed in similar fashion, no better plan of engagement could have been devised than the one Hannibal then arranged
problem: παραπλησίῳ καθοπλισμῷ χρώμενον is accusative singular, agreeing with the unexpressed general who arranges the battle, not with Ῥωμαίους (plural). The similar equipment belongs to the hypothetical general (i.e. one with arms comparable to Hannibal's), not to the Romans.
proposed_fix: no one using comparable equipment could have arranged a better engagement against the Romans than the one Hannibal then arranged

quote: had returned to it only after more than forty-five years
problem: πλείω δὲ τῶν πέντε καὶ τετταράκοντ᾽ ἐτῶν ἔχων εἰς αὐτὴν ἐπανήκει: ἔχων + years gives his age. He came back when he was over forty-five years old, not after forty-five years away. He left at nine (ἐνναέτης), so he was gone for about thirty-six years.
proposed_fix: was now returning to it at more than forty-five years of age

quote: I think you would find no one among us better suited to stand beside you and help you.
problem: μηδένα συναγωνιστὴν καὶ συνεργὸν ἄλλον εὑρεῖν ἂν ἡμῶν ἐπιτηδειότερον: ἡμῶν is a genitive of comparison ('no one ... more suitable than me'). Polybius is offering himself; 'among us' turns his offer into a general remark.
proposed_fix: I think you would find no one better suited than me to stand beside you and help you.

quote: This ambition first came into prominence at the time we are speaking of,
problem: συνέβη δὲ τὴν παροῦσαν αἵρεσιν οἷον ἐκλάμψαι: 'the present tendency' is the extravagance just described (Macedonian wealth and unrivalled power are given as its causes), not Scipio's ambition. Also, πρῶτον μὲν introduces the first reason; it does not mean the tendency 'first' appeared then.
proposed_fix: This tendency blazed out, as it were, at the time we are speaking of,

quote: Scipio gave to his mother, who had long since been separated from Lucius
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: ἐδωρήσατο τῇ μητρί, *** ᾗ συνέβαινε κεχωρίσθαι. The English reads straight through without marking the gap (editors usually supply her name, Papiria).
proposed_fix: Scipio gave to his mother [...], who had long since been separated from Lucius

quote: But when he insisted that Scipio had given exactly those instructions, they believed him and went on to the young man
problem: διαπιστήσαντες προῆγον ἐπὶ τὸν νεανίσκον: διαπιστήσαντες means 'disbelieving'. They did not believe the banker, and that is why they went to Scipio. The English reverses this.
proposed_fix: But when he insisted that Scipio had given exactly those instructions, they did not believe him and went on to the young man

quote: After this, he was obliged to pay the remaining half of the dowries owed to the daughters of Scipio the Great, who were the sisters of his adoptive father.
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: ἀδελφαῖς δὲ τοῦ κατὰ θέσιν πατρός, *** λαβόντος, αὐτὸν ἔδει. A genitive participle clause (someone 'having received/inherited') is lost. The English smooths over it.
proposed_fix: After this, he was obliged to pay the remaining half of the dowries owed to the daughters of Scipio the Great, who were the sisters of his adoptive father [...].

quote: by taking back a city that had often disputed control with them
problem: ταύτην ἐπανελομένους = 'by destroying/doing away with' the city, not 'taking back'.
proposed_fix: by destroying a city that had often disputed control with them

quote: but arriving at the same end through the appearances they displayed
problem: ἥξειν δ᾽ ἐπὶ ταὐτὸ τέλος ἐκ τῶν προφαινομένων = 'but would reach the same end, to judge from present indications' (future, a prediction), not a completed arrival 'through appearances they displayed'.
proposed_fix: but bound, to judge from present indications, to reach the same end

quote: For since nothing irreparable had happened on account of them, they had resolved in a harsh and irreversible way against them, willing to accept and endure anything in order to carry out what had been ordered.
problem: μηδενὸς ... γεγονότος is concessive ('although the Carthaginians had done nothing irreparable'), and the genitive absolute πᾶν ἀναδεχομένων καὶ πᾶν ὑπομενόντων ποιήσειν τὸ προσταττόμενον refers to the Carthaginians (who accepted every condition and submitted to do whatever was ordered), not the Romans.
proposed_fix: For although the Carthaginians had done nothing irreparable, the Romans had taken an irreparable and harsh decision against them, even though they accepted every condition and submitted to do whatever was ordered.

quote: gradually revealing one demand and concealing another
problem: τὰ μὲν προτείνοντες, τὰ δὲ παραγυμνοῦντες = 'putting forward some demands and disclosing others'; παραγυμνοῦντες means uncovering, not concealing (contrast ἐπικρυπτομένους earlier).
proposed_fix: gradually putting forward one demand and disclosing another

quote: for when the Carthaginians had handed themselves over, the Romans had simply done what they wished, since those surrendering were no longer obeying orders, and had thus brought necessity upon them
problem: λαβόντας γὰρ τὴν ἐπιτροπὴν παρ᾽ ἑκόντων ὃ βούλοιντο πράττειν = 'having received from willing parties the authority to do what they wished'; the Romans received authority, they did not 'simply do what they wished'. οὐ πειθαρχούντων = 'when they did not obey' (no 'no longer').
proposed_fix: for having received from the Carthaginians, of their own free will, the authority to do whatever they wished, the Romans, when the Carthaginians did not obey their orders, had thus brought compulsion to bear on them

quote: we no longer had any need at all
problem: μηκέτι χρείαν ἡμῶν εἶναι μηδεμίαν = 'there was no longer any need of us at all' (Polybius was no longer needed), not that 'we' had no needs.
proposed_fix: there was no longer any need of us at all

quote: Aulus Maninus
problem: Αὖλος Μαγκῖνος = Aulus Mancinus.
proposed_fix: Aulus Mancinus

quote: Lucius Malloelus
problem: Λεύκιος Μαλλέολος = Lucius Malleolus.
proposed_fix: Lucius Malleolus

quote: Prusias would arrive not only already dead, but that Nicomedes too would grow old in his kingdom before the embassy could ever get there
problem: συμβήσεται μὴ μόνον ἀπολόμενον φθάσαι τὸν Προυσίαν = 'not only would Prusias be dead before they arrived' — Prusias is not the one arriving; the envoys are.
proposed_fix: not only would Prusias be dead before the embassy arrived, but Nicomedes too would have grown old on his throne

quote: but also to seek punishment from him
problem: τιμωρίαν βούλεσθαι παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λαμβάνειν = 'to wish to take vengeance on him'; the English can be read as the people wanting to be punished by him.
proposed_fix: but also to wish to take vengeance on him

quote: he preserved his whole life and left his kingdom free from every plot and every domestic stain
problem: διετήρησε τὸν ὅλον βίον ... ἄμοιρον αὑτοῦ γενέσθαι τὴν βασιλείαν = 'throughout his whole life he kept his kingdom free from' plots; τὸν ὅλον βίον is duration, not the object 'preserved his life'.
proposed_fix: he kept his kingdom, throughout his whole life, free from every plot and every domestic stain

quote: extensive and fully fruitful estates in separate allotments
problem: μυριοπλέθρους ἀγροὺς = estates of ten thousand plethra each; the number is smoothed into 'extensive'.
proposed_fix: fully fruitful estates of ten thousand plethra each in separate allotments

quote: Micypsa
problem: Μικίψης = Micipsa (standard form).
proposed_fix: Micipsa

quote: but sought to raise only one or two, and hardly even those,
problem: ἀλλὰ μόλις ἓν τῶν πλείστων ἢ δύο ... θρέψαι: μόλις means 'at most / barely' one or two (out of the many born). It does not mean they 'hardly' raised even those one or two. The added restriction misreads μόλις.
proposed_fix: but raised at most one or two of the many born,

quote: released from great internal strife and civil slaughter through Roman favor.
problem: The Greek breaks off here: διὰ τῆς Ῥωμαίων... φιλοτ̣ιμίας:... followed by a fragmentary clause (ἅμα δυσμενείας μὲν ἢ βλάβης τῆς ἐν τοῖς πρότερον καιροῖς πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ...). The English closes the sentence with no gap marked before the next fragment.
proposed_fix: released from great internal strife and civil slaughter through Roman generosity [...] [fragmentary text follows] [...]

quote: whereas in the earlier days, under the kings who were truly kings, they had already experienced [...]
problem: πλείστους ... φυγαδευθέντας καὶ στρεβλωθέντας καὶ φονευθέντας ἢ τῶν ἐν τοῖς πρότερον καιροῖς ὑπὸ τῶν κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν βασι[λέων]: ἢ is comparative. They saw more of their people exiled, tortured and killed in a short time than under the true kings in earlier times. 'whereas ... they had already experienced' turns the comparison into a contrast, and the clause is built from fragmentary words (ἤδη τοῦτο γε ε̣χ̣...) that belong to the lacuna.
proposed_fix: more than in earlier times under the true kings [...]

quote: they were angered at the Roman encampment itself and regretted their former wrongs against themselves [...] [fragmentary text continues].
problem: The Greek reads only ...Ῥωμαίων στρατοπεδεύματος ἐξ αὐτῆς μεταμέλοι: ἐν ἀδικ... τῶν πρὸ τοῦ Ψευδοφιλίππου μὲν εἰς αὐτοὺς παρανομημάτων. There is no 'angered'. The παρανομήματα are lawless acts committed against them (εἰς αὐτούς) before the Pseudo-Philip, not 'their' wrongs. The English also leaves out the legible sentence after the gap: ... πολλῶν τε μετὰ μὲν τοῦ Δημητρίου καὶ πάλιν μετὰ Περσέως μαχόμενοι πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἡττήθησαν, ἀνδρὶ δὲ στυγνῷ συναγωνιζόμενοι καὶ περὶ τῆς τούτου βασιλείας ἀνδραγαθήσαντες ἐνίκησαν Ῥωμαίους. This μὲν ... δέ contrast is the puzzle that the next sentence ('who would not be puzzled') refers to. The MS has Δημητρίου, kept as transmitted (historically one expects Philip V); the name is not emended here.
proposed_fix: [...] the Roman camp [...] regret [...] the lawless acts committed against them before the Pseudo-Philip [...]. [...] And though they had fought against the Romans with Demetrius, and again with Perseus, and been defeated, yet fighting alongside a hateful man and showing courage in defense of his kingship, they defeated the Romans.

quote: and no one defended this act as just.
problem: The sentence runs across the chapter seam: διεδικαίου δὲ τὴν πρᾶξιν ταύτην οὐδεὶς | Ἀλεξάνδρου (first word of ch. 3) = 'no one justified this act of Alexander's'. The genitive belongs here, not at the start of ch. 3.
proposed_fix: and no one defended this act of Alexander’s as just.

quote: After Alexander’s campaign, they therefore, after a short time and with some help received, once again lived in their homeland in safety.
problem: 'After Alexander's campaign' is invented from the seam word Ἀλεξάνδρου, which ends the previous chapter's sentence (τὴν πρᾶξιν ταύτην οὐδεὶς Ἀλεξάνδρου). This sentence is just τοιγαροῦν βραχεῖ χρόνῳ τυχόντες ἐπικουρίας τινὸς αὖθις ᾤκουν τὴν πατρίδα μετ᾽ ἀσφαλείας.
proposed_fix: Therefore, after a short time, receiving some help, they once again lived in their homeland in safety.

quote: For all who fall into unexpected disasters should be counted as unfortunate, both collectively and individually;
problem: The μὲν … δέ contrast is between ἀκληρεῖν ('to be unlucky', all who meet unexpected calamities) and ἀτυχεῖν ('to be unfortunate', only those disgraced by their own folly). Translating both as 'unfortunate' turns the distinction into a contradiction.
proposed_fix: For all who fall into unexpected disasters, both collectively and individually, should be counted as unlucky;

quote: Peloponnesians, Boeotians, Phocians, Locrians,
problem: Lacuna smoothed: Greek reads Φωκεῖς, ... εῖς, Λοκροί — an ethnic ending in -εῖς is lost between Phocians and Locrians (often restored as Euboeans).
proposed_fix: Peloponnesians, Boeotians, Phocians, [...], Locrians,

quote: Not only in number, but in every way, they were not merely unfortunate in the ordinary sense, but suffered a shameful sort of misfortune, as dishonorable as possible.
problem: Lacunae smoothed: ... μὴ μόνον κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος ... τῶν πρότερον, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ ... ἐπίπαν — gaps before and inside the phrase, and 'in every way' is invented. Also negation softened: οὐκ ἠκλήρησαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἠτύχησαν = 'they were NOT (merely) unlucky but suffered misfortune'; 'not merely unfortunate' blurs the ἀκληρεῖν/ἀτυχεῖν distinction just defined.
proposed_fix: [...] not only in the number [...] of earlier ones, but also in [...]; in a word, they were not unlucky but suffered a misfortune as shameful and disgraceful as could be.

quote: Thus, stripped of all good things, some perished from hunger, while others, driven to desperation, even then took rods and axes into the cities [...]
problem: Lacunae smoothed and text invented: Greek is ... ἅμα. τοιγαροῦν στερηθέντες πάντων τῶν καλῶν οἱ μὲν ὑπὸ στέ[...], ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ δ[...]ντες εἰς τὰς πόλεις τότε παρεδέξαντο ῥάβδους καὶ πελέκεις ἐθελο[...]. 'perished from hunger' and 'driven to desperation' have no basis in the fragments. παρεδέξαντο = 'admitted/received' (the Roman fasces into their cities), not 'took'; ἐθελο- suggests 'willingly' but is broken.
proposed_fix: [...] Thus, deprived of all good things, some [...], while others [...] then admitted the rods and axes into their cities [...]

quote: because of the excess of their own mistakes, if it is right to say so.
problem: εἰ χρὴ λέγειν ἰδίων qualifies the word 'own' specifically ('if one should call them their own'), which the next γάρ-sentence explains (the many were misled; the leaders were guilty). 'if it is right to say so' loses the point.
proposed_fix: because of the excess of their own mistakes—if one should call them their own.

quote: when it was above all right to conceal the mistakes of the Greeks.
problem: οἷς καθῆκον ἦν μάλιστα πάντων περιστέλλειν refers to the writer (ἡμῖν): critics will say that I, of all people, ought to cover up the Greeks' faults. The impersonal English loses whose duty it was.
proposed_fix: when I, of all people, ought to have concealed the mistakes of the Greeks.

quote: For the more widely the transmission of what is written reaches people, and the longer it lasts,
problem: The ὅσῳ … τοσούτῳ clause compares written record with speech: ἡ διὰ τῶν ὑπομνημάτων παράδοσις τῶν πρὸς καιρὸν λεγομένων = 'written transmission, compared with what is said for the occasion'. The comparand is dropped.
proposed_fix: For the more widely, and the longer, written record reaches than words spoken for the moment,

quote: But those who love learning seek continuity and look forward to hearing the end of the account;
problem: ζητεῖν δὲ τοὺς φιλομαθοῦντας … ἱμείρειν … συνεκτρέχειν are infinitives still governed by φάσκοντες: this is the critics' claim, which Polybius then rejects (ἐμοὶ δ᾽ οὐχ οὕτως δοκεῖ). 'But' presents it as the author's own view.
proposed_fix: And, they say, those who love learning seek continuity and long to hear the end of the subject;

quote: rests for those who labor hard [...]
problem: Not a lacuna: the phrase is completed by ἀνδρῶν, printed as the first word of ch. 6 (τοῖς φιλοπόνοις τῶν | ἀνδρῶν = 'for industrious men'). The gap marker is false.
proposed_fix: rests for men who love hard work.

quote: For those who are diligent in such matters, the greatest historians of old seem to me
problem: 'For those who are diligent in such matters' is invented from the seam word ἀνδρῶν, which ends ch. 5's sentence. The sentence begins διὸ καὶ τῶν ἀρχαίων συγγραφέων οἱ λογιώτατοι = 'That is why the most learned of the ancient historians'; the inferential διό is lost.
proposed_fix: That is why the most learned of the ancient historians seem to me

quote: and to take responsibility for everything, since we will do what is ordered
problem: πᾶν ἀναδέχεσθαι διότι ποιήσομεν τὸ προσταττόμενον: διότι here means 'that' (content clause after ἀναδέχεσθαι, 'guarantee that'), not causal 'since'.
proposed_fix: and to guarantee that we will do everything that is ordered

quote: Hasdrubal said that he did not understand him.
problem: ὁ δ᾽ Ἀσδρούβας ἀγνοεῖν αὐτὸν ἔφη: Hasdrubal said that Gulussa (αὐτόν, subject of ἀγνοεῖν) was mistaken / did not know the situation; the following καὶ γάρ explains what Gulussa does not know. The English reverses who is ignorant.
proposed_fix: Hasdrubal said that Gulussa was mistaken.

quote: or the troops outside the walls, saying that they were safe;
problem: οὐ γάρ πω … ἠκηκόει … τὰ περὶ τῶν ὑπαίθρων δυνάμεων [ὅτι σώζονται]: this is the narrator's aside (he had not yet heard the news about the forces in the field); ὅτι σώζονται is bracketed as suspect by the editor and in any case is not something Hasdrubal 'says'. The English attributes a doubtful phrase to Hasdrubal's speech.
proposed_fix: or the forces in the field;

quote: For they would not, he said, allow themselves to be seen openly violating a truce, but would give many opportunities for salvation.
problem: οὐ γὰρ περιόψεσθαι σφᾶς προφανῶς παρασπονδουμένους: the gods would not stand by and watch them (the Carthaginians, σφᾶς) being openly wronged in breach of the treaty. The English inverts it, making the gods the would-be treaty-breakers.
proposed_fix: For the gods, he said, would not stand by and see them so openly wronged in breach of the treaty, but would give them many opportunities for salvation.

quote: that among the Greeks and among the Carthaginians of that time one would not easily find two men more alike as masters of affairs
problem: προστάτας πραγμάτων ὁμοιοτέρους τῶν παρὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησι τότε καὶ παρὰ τοῖς Καρχηδονίοις ὑπαρξάντων οὐκ ἂν εὕροι τις ῥᾳδίως: genitive of comparison — one would not easily find leaders more alike than those the Greeks and Carthaginians had at that time. Plural leaders, not 'two men', and not a search 'among' them.
proposed_fix: that one would not easily find leaders of affairs more alike than those who led the Greeks and the Carthaginians at that time

quote: When the envoys who had come from the Peloponnese to Aurelius arrived
problem: παραγενομένων ἐκ Πελοποννήσου τῶν περὶ τὸν Αὐρήλιον πρεσβευτῶν: the envoys are Aurelius and his colleagues, returning from the Peloponnese to Rome; they were not sent 'to Aurelius'.
proposed_fix: When Aurelius and his fellow envoys arrived from the Peloponnese

quote: assumed that the Romans were acting with hypocrisy because the war in Carthage was still unfinished
problem: ὑπελάμβανον καθ᾽ ὑπόκρισιν τοὺς Ῥωμαίους *** διὰ τὸ μένειν ἀτελῆ τὰ κατὰ Καρχηδόνα: the Greek has a lacuna where the verb of the infinitive clause stood; the English supplies 'were acting' as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: assumed that the Romans [...] by way of pretense, because the war against Carthage was still unfinished

quote: the justice of what the envoys from Sextus were saying
problem: τοῖς ὑπὸ τῶν περὶ τὸν Σέξτον λεγομένοις δικαίοις: Sextus and his colleagues are themselves the Roman envoys; not 'envoys from Sextus'.
proposed_fix: the justice of what Sextus and his colleagues were saying

quote: men who had been deliberately selected as the worst from every city
problem: οὗτοι δ᾽ ἦσαν ὥσπερ ἐπίτηδες ἐξ ἑκάστης πόλεως κατ᾽ ἐκλογὴν οἱ χείριστοι: ὥσπερ ('as if') makes it a comparison — they were the worst of each city, as though picked on purpose; the English states as fact that they were deliberately selected.
proposed_fix: men who were the worst of every city, as if picked out on purpose

quote: and there confer with the Lacedaemonians so that some agreed settlement
problem: κοινολογηθέντες τοῖς Λακεδαιμονίοις ***, ἵνα γένηταί τις ὡμολογημένη λύσις: lacuna after Λακεδαιμονίοις (the main verb of the reported reply is lost); the English reads on as if whole.
proposed_fix: and there confer with the Lacedaemonians [...] so that some agreed settlement

quote: For it was necessary, he said, not for the Lacedaemonians or the Romans to be troubled in this way, but rather for those among their own people who cooperated with the enemy;
problem: δεῖν γὰρ οὐ Λακεδαιμονίους οὐδὲ Ῥωμαίους ἀγωνιᾶν οὕτως ὡς τοὺς ἐξ αὐτῶν συνεργοῦντας τοῖς ἐχθροῖς: the accusatives are the objects of ἀγωνιᾶν (to fear / be anxious about), with οὐ … οὕτως ὡς = 'not so much … as'. The Achaeans should fear not the Lacedaemonians or Romans so much as the traitors among them. The English makes the Lacedaemonians and Romans the ones who are troubled, which inverts the sense.
proposed_fix: For they ought not to fear the Lacedaemonians or the Romans so much as those among their own people who cooperated with the enemy;

quote: Philataerus
problem: The Greek has Φιλεταίρου, i.e. Philetaerus (the Attalid brother of Eumenes II). The English misspells the name.
proposed_fix: Philetaerus

quote: a total of ten thousand men
problem: εἰς μυρίους καὶ δισχιλίους = to the number of twelve thousand (10,000 + 2,000).
proposed_fix: a total of twelve thousand men

quote: was driven from the country
problem: ἠλᾶτο κατὰ τῆς χώρας = he wandered about the country, meaning within the Peloponnese he had withdrawn to. The English says he was expelled from it, which inverts the sense.
proposed_fix: wandered about the country

quote: For though they clearly knew what they had done
problem: σαφῶς γὰρ σφίσι τὰ πεπραγμένα συνειδότες is causal: it is because they were conscious of what they had done that they could not believe they would find mercy. The English 'though' turns the causal participle into a concession, which reverses the logic.
proposed_fix: For since they clearly knew what they had done

quote: even though they were all equally in the wrong
problem: εἰ καὶ πάντων ἅμα διήμαρτον: πάντων is the genitive of the thing missed with διαμαρτάνω ('even though they failed of everything at once / missed the mark entirely'). It is not a subject 'they all'. The English misreads the construction.
proposed_fix: even though they failed utterly in everything

quote: but believed that Philon was speaking because he privately placed his own interest and security above everything else
problem: ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοὺς κατ᾽ ἰδίαν τὸ σφέτερον συμφέρον … τιθεμένους ταῦτα λέγειν: the plural αὐτοὺς … τιθεμένους refers to those urging acceptance (Stratius and his associates, possibly with Philon), and the councillors mean their own private interest. The Greek does not single out Philon. The English names the wrong referent.
proposed_fix: but believed that those urging this were speaking because they privately placed their own interest and security above everything else

quote: so that the enemy could not cross and fight from the embankments
problem: ὅπως μὴ διαβαίνοντες οἱ πολέμιοι προσμάχωνται τοῖς χώμασιν: so that the enemy could not wade across and attack the moles/embankments (the Roman works). The English reverses the direction of the action.
proposed_fix: so that the enemy could not cross and attack the embankments

quote: an overbearing man must never say or do anything proud
problem: δεῖ μηδέποτε λέγειν μηδὲ πράττειν μηδὲν ὑπερήφανον ἄνθρωπον ὄντα: one must never, being human (mortal), say or do anything arrogant. ἄνθρωπον ὄντα is 'being a man', not 'an overbearing man'; the English garbles the moral.
proposed_fix: one who is only human must never say or do anything arrogant

quote: because not only she herself but also the children were being saved from his fate
problem: διότι τὸ μὲν ἐκείνου μέρος οὐκ αὐτὴ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ τέκνα σῴζεται: because, so far as it lay with him (the general), not only she but the children were saved. τὸ ἐκείνου μέρος is 'as far as he was concerned', not 'from his fate'.
proposed_fix: because, as far as it rested with him, not only she herself but also the children were being saved

quote: after saying that she herself would obtain no private salvation from the general by deserting, he could
problem: πῶς αὐτῇ μὲν φάσκων οὐδὲν κατ᾽ ἰδίαν παρὰ τοῦ στρατηγοῦ πορίζοιτο τὴν σωτηρίαν αὐτομολήσας: how, saying nothing to her (αὐτῇ οὐδὲν φάσκων), he had deserted and privately procured his own safety from the general. The subject of πορίζοιτο is Hasdrubal; the negation belongs to 'saying nothing to her', not to her obtaining safety. Sense inverted.
proposed_fix: without saying a word to her, he had deserted and privately secured his own safety from the general, and how he could

quote: he dared now to sit here crowned, while he had many times said that the day would never come when he would see Hasdrubal alive
problem: πῶς δὲ παρὰ τούτοις τολμᾷ καθῆσθαι νῦν θαλλοὺς ἔχων πρὸς οὓς... πολλάκις οὐδέποτε ταύτην ἔσεσθαι τὴν ἡμέραν, ἐν ᾗ συμβήσεται τὸν ἥλιον ἅμα καθορᾶν Ἀσδρούβαν ζῶντα: he sits beside these men (παρὰ τούτοις) holding suppliant branches (θαλλούς), men to whom (πρὸς οὓς) he had often [gap; verb of saying lost] that the day would never come when the sun (τὸν ἥλιον) would see Hasdrubal alive and his country burning. English smooths the lacuna after πρὸς οὓς, drops 'to these men', and makes 'he' rather than the sun the seer.
proposed_fix: he dared now to sit beside these men holding suppliant branches, men to whom he had [...] many times that the day would never come when the sun would see Hasdrubal alive

quote: [...] The text here is badly broken in the witness, but the sense is that Polybius is completing Scipio’s remark about the danger of overconfidence and the importance of good judgment.
problem: Only the opening lines are broken. The Greek then has a fully legible passage that the English omits: καὶ τοῦτ᾽ εἴρηται παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ· καὶ ἐπιστρέψας ἐξ αὐτῆς καὶ λαβόμενός μου τῆς δεξιᾶς 'ὦ Πολύβιε,' ἔφη 'καλὸν μέν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως ἐγὼ δέδια καὶ προορῶμαι μή ποτέ τις ἄλλος τοῦτο τὸ παράγγελμα δώσει περὶ τῆς ἡμετέρας πατρίδος.' ταύτης δὲ [gap]. The summary also misattributes: it is Scipio who speaks, to Polybius. Intact text treated as lacuna; the real gap after ταύτης δὲ is not marked.
proposed_fix: [...] The opening lines are badly broken in the witness; Polybius is speaking, and a saying of the poet is cited. [...] And at once he turned and grasped my right hand and said, “Polybius, it is a fine thing; but somehow I fear and foresee that someday someone else will give this same order about our own country.” Of this [...]

quote: For as he went through the cities to sell the property of all who had been associated with Diaeus, he was doing so also for men who had been convicted, except for those who had children or parents.
problem: The subject τοῦτον is the treasurer (ὁ ταμίας), not Polybius; in the English 'he' reads as Polybius. Also τῶν καὶ κατακριθέντων describes the same group (Diaeus' associates who had also been condemned), not a second group: πωλεῖν τὰς οὐσίας πάντων τῶν τῷ Διαίῳ κοινωνησάντων, τῶν καὶ κατακριθέντων, ὅσοι μὴ παῖδας ἢ γονέας εἶχον.
proposed_fix: For the treasurer was going through the cities selling the property of all who had been associated with Diaeus and had also been condemned, so far as they had no children or parents.

quote: When these arrangements had been completed, the ten commissioners,
problem: Number omitted: ταῦτα δὲ διοικήσαντες ἐν ἓξ μησὶν οἱ δέκα — they completed these arrangements in six months.
proposed_fix: When they had completed these arrangements in six months, the ten commissioners,

quote: After the Roman general had separated from the assembly in Achaea,
problem: μετὰ τὸ χωρισθῆναι ἐξ Ἀχαΐας τὸ συνέδριον: the subject of the departure is the council (the ten commissioners), which left Achaea; the general did not separate from an assembly.
proposed_fix: After the council of commissioners had departed from Achaea, the Roman general

quote: the Eleans and Neapolitans
problem: Greek has Ἐλεατῶν, the people of Elea (Velia) in Italy alongside Tarentines, Locrians and Neapolitans; 'Eleans' means the people of Elis in the Peloponnese, a different place.
proposed_fix: the people of Elea and the Neapolitans

quote: twenty-four feet high and a foot wide in diameter
problem: Greek: κατὰ δὲ τὸ πλάτος τριῶν παλαιστῶν ἔχων τὴν διάμετρον, i.e. three palms in diameter (about nine inches), not a foot.
proposed_fix: twenty-four feet high and three palms (about nine inches) in diameter

quote: ten ships of matching speed
problem: Greek has ἔχων δέκα ναῦς ὁμοπλοούσας, 'ten ships sailing together / in company'; nothing about matching speed.
proposed_fix: ten ships sailing in company with him

quote: complete discouragement and famine: discouragement because of the panic, and famine partly because of the numbers gathered there and partly because they expected a siege
problem: Greek: δυσθυμία καὶ λιμὸς ἦν ὁλοσχερής, τὰ μὲν διὰ τὸ πλῆθος, τὰ δὲ διὰ τὴν προσδοκίαν τῆς πολιορκίας. The τὰ μὲν … τὰ δέ pair covers both distress and famine together; 'because of the panic' is not a separate cause in this clause (the fear is already in διὰ τὸν φόβον earlier).
proposed_fix: complete discouragement and famine, partly because of the numbers gathered there and partly because they expected a siege

quote: made their way with difficulty back to Aspis
problem: Greek: διέπεσον εἰς τὴν Ἀσπίδα παραδόξως. παραδόξως means unexpectedly / against expectation, not 'with difficulty'.
proposed_fix: made their way, against all expectation, to Aspis

quote: and because, too, one threatening constellation had not yet set while another was on the point of rising
problem: Greek: τὴν μὲν οὐδέπω καταλήγειν ἐπισημασίαν, τὴν δ᾽ ἐπιφέρεσθαι. ἐπισημασία is a spell of stormy weather (signalled by a star's rising/setting), not a constellation; one such stormy period had not yet ended and the next was coming on.
proposed_fix: and because, too, one spell of stormy weather had not yet ended while another was coming on

quote: vying with one another for Hasdrubal’s favor
problem: ἀντιφιλοδοξοῦντες πρὸς τὸν Ἀσδρούβαν: the elephant-masters were rivalling Hasdrubal (competing with him for credit), not competing with one another for his favor; the next clause (βουλόμενοι δι᾽ αὑτῶν ποιῆσαι τὸ προτέρημα) confirms they wanted the success to be their own rather than the commander's.
proposed_fix: in rivalry with Hasdrubal

quote: he immediately sent them out together with his own men. To deal with the Gauls he sent Hannibal
problem: εὐθέως μετ᾽ αὐτῶν ἀπέστειλε πρὸς μὲν τοὺς Κελτοὺς Ἀννίβαν…: μετ᾽ αὐτῶν means Hannibal and Alexon were sent along with the loyal officers (αὐτῶν = the officers who accepted his words); there are no 'his own men' in the Greek.
proposed_fix: he immediately sent them out, and along with them he sent to the Gauls Hannibal

quote: the leading friend of Adherbal
problem: φίλος Ἀτάρβου πρῶτος: the name is Ἀτάρβας (Atarbas), not Adherbal (Ἀδέρβας), a different person.
proposed_fix: the leading friend of Atarbas

quote: an internal war broke out to receive the Romans—the one against the people called the Faliscans
problem: ἐξεδέξατο γάρ πόλεμος ἐμφύλιος Ῥωμαίους μέν ... καρχηδονίους δέ: ἐξεδέξατο means 'succeeded/followed' (the war followed the settlement, for the Romans on one side, for the Carthaginians on the other, μέν ... δέ). 'Broke out to receive the Romans' garbles the verb and the μέν ... δέ parallel with the Carthaginian clause.
proposed_fix: an internal war followed for the Romans—the one against the people called the Faliscans

quote: neither gave them up nor allowed it; they warned those present
problem: Greek is οἱ δ᾽ οὔτ᾽ ἔδοσαν, προεῖπόν τε τοῖς παροῦσιν: they did not give (the bodies) and (te) warned those present. There is no second negated verb 'allowed it'; the English invents one and splits the sentence wrongly.
proposed_fix: did not give them up, and they warned those present

quote: at the same period as the so-called Phlegraean plains around Capua and Nola—plains which
problem: Greek: καθ᾽ οὓς χρόνους καὶ τὰ Φλέγραιά ποτε καλούμενα τὰ περὶ Καπύην καὶ Νώλην — the Phlegraean plains are a second object of ἐνέμοντο (the Etruscans held them too, at the time), not a term of temporal comparison.
proposed_fix: at the time when they also held the once so-called Phlegraean plains around Capua and Nola—plains which

quote: those lying toward the eastern part of the Po
problem: Greek: περὶ τὰς ἀνατολὰς τοῦ Πάδου — ἀνατολαί of the river means its rising/sources (the Laoi and Lebecii are the westernmost, near the Po's source), not its 'eastern part'; the Greek word is open to 'risings' but 'eastern part' reverses the geography.
proposed_fix: those lying around the sources of the Po

quote: The Roman shields, that is, offered far greater protection, and their swords were far more effective in action, while the Gallic sword could only deliver a downward cut.
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: οἱ μὲν οὖν θυρεοὶ πρὸς ἀσφάλειαν, αἱ δὲ μάχαιραι πρὸς πρᾶξιν μεγάλην διαφορὰν **** ἔχειν, τὴν δὲ Γαλατικὴν καταφορὰν ἔχειν μόνον. The text breaks off after μεγάλην διαφορὰν, and the English reads on as if the sentence were whole, supplying 'far greater' and 'far more effective' (comparatives that are not in the Greek).
proposed_fix: The shields, for protection, and the swords, for effective action, [...] made a great difference [text missing in the Greek], while the Gallic sword has only the downward cut.

quote: may exhaust all their own resources before yielding any of what is essential
problem: The Greek is πάσας ἐξελέγχωσι τὰς σφετέρας ἐλπίδας: 'put all their own hopes to the test'. ἐλπίδας is 'hopes', not 'resources'. The English changes the object and the sense.
proposed_fix: may put all their own hopes to the test before yielding any of what is essential

quote: relieved the Achaeans of their gravest problem
problem: τοὺς δ᾽ Ἀχαιοὺς ἀπέλυσε τοῦ μεγίστου προβλήματος: πρόβλημα is a thing thrown up in front, a bulwark or barrier (here Corinth/the Isthmus defence), not a 'problem' in the modern sense. 'Problem' makes the Achaeans simply benefit; the Greek says Cleomenes freed (stripped) them of their greatest bulwark, which then paradoxically gave them the pretext of the next sentence.
proposed_fix: relieved the Achaeans of their greatest bulwark

quote: the killing of fellow citizens he treats as the gravest impiety, deserving the heaviest penalties
problem: τὸ γε τοὺς πολίτας ἀποκτεινύναι μέγιστον ἀσέβημα τίθεται καὶ μεγίστων ἄξιον προστίμων: τίθεται is passive/impersonal (is held, is regarded), a general opinion, not a view attributed to the historian or to Phylarchus.
proposed_fix: the killing of fellow citizens is held to be the gravest impiety, deserving the heaviest penalties

quote: In the one, what governs is plausibility, even if it be false, because the object is the deception of the spectators; in the other it is the truth
problem: ἐν ἐκείνοις μὲν ἡγεῖται τὸ πιθανόν ... ἐν δὲ τούτοις τἀληθές: ἐκεῖνοι = tragedy (plausibility), οὗτοι = history (truth). After 'the latter ... the former' in the preceding sentence, 'the one/the other' can be read the wrong way round.
proposed_fix: In tragedy, what governs is plausibility, even if it be false, because the object is the deception of the spectators; in history it is the truth

quote: they suffered utter ruin for their homeland because of their loyalty to the Achaeans
problem: ὁλοσχερῶς ἔπταισαν τῇ πατρίδι: they were utterly ruined/came to grief as regards their country (lost it), because of their choice of the Achaeans. 'For their homeland' reads as on behalf of it, which is not what the dative says.
proposed_fix: they were utterly ruined in respect of their homeland because of their choice of the Achaeans

quote: For a long while the Romans paid no attention to them, but at this point they dispatched envoys
problem: Greek: Ῥωμαῖοι δὲ πλεονάκις αὐτῶν παρακηκοότες τότε πρεσβευτὰς ἐξαπέστειλαν. πλεονάκις means 'several times / repeatedly', not 'for a long while'; παρακηκοότες with genitive is 'having heard (from them)'. Sense 'paid no attention' is a possible but uncertain reading of παρακούω, and the duration is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: The Romans, who had heard from them several times already, at this point dispatched envoys

quote: in the territory of whichever is at war
problem: Greek ἐν τῇ τῶν πολεμουμένων χώρᾳ means in the territory of those being warred upon (the party attacked), not simply whichever party is at war.
proposed_fix: in the territory of whichever is being attacked

quote: they do not dare to face us head-on
problem: Greek: ὅτι μόνον οὐ τολμῶσι κατὰ πρόσωπον ἰδεῖν ἡμᾶς. μόνον οὐ means 'all but / very nearly', so the Carthaginians all but do not dare; the English states it flatly and drops the hedge.
proposed_fix: they all but do not dare to face us head-on

quote: he encamped near the place called Vibo
problem: Greek has τὸ καλούμενον Οἰβώνιον (Oebonium/Vibinum in Daunia, in Apulia). 'Vibo' reads as Vibo Valentia in Bruttium, a different place far to the south.
proposed_fix: he encamped near the place called Oebonium

quote: When the Romans were already close at hand, they gave the signal for battle and put out to sea, having resolved to fight.
problem: The genitive absolute ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῶν Ῥωμαίων σύνεγγυς ὄντων leaves the subject of σημήναντες ... ἀνήγοντο, κρίναντες ναυμαχεῖν as Hasdrubal's men (οἱ περὶ τὸν Ἀσδρούβαν), i.e. the Carthaginians. The English 'they' after 'the Romans' reads as the Romans putting out, and the following 'before long they began to give way' (πρὸς τὸ κλίνειν ὥρμησαν) is the Carthaginians, so the identity of the subject is inverted.
proposed_fix: When the Romans were already close at hand, the Carthaginians gave the signal for battle and put out to sea, having resolved to fight.

quote: handled every detail according to their judgment
problem: Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἐκείνων γνώμην, where ἐκείνων = the consuls (τῶν ὑπάτων), not Gnaeus and his officers (contrast earlier κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν γνώμην). English 'their' reads as the officers' own judgment, inverting the sense.
proposed_fix: handled every detail according to the consuls' judgment

quote: regarding nothing as belonging to others and everything as theirs to plunder
problem: Greek: οὐδὲν οἰκεῖον, πάντα δ᾽ ἡγούμενοι πολέμια. οἰκεῖον means 'friendly/kindred', opposed to πολέμια 'hostile': they regard nothing as friendly and everything as hostile. The English inverts/misreads the antithesis.
proposed_fix: regarding nothing as friendly and everything as hostile

quote: he had in effect handed over the whole of his command to Dorimachus
problem: Greek: παρακεχωρήκει τούτῳ τῆς ὅλης ἀρχῆς, after 'Δωριμάχου καὶ Σκόπα'. τούτῳ is singular and its antecedent is ambiguous; the nearest name is Scopas, and Scopas is the one who leads the action that follows. The English silently resolves it to Dorimachus. The singular may be a corruption of τούτοις (both).
proposed_fix: he had in effect handed over the whole of his command to the latter

quote: saying that it was not possible to admit any new member apart from Philip and the other allies
problem: Greek: οὐ φάσκοντες δυνατὸν εἶναι χωρὶς Φιλίππου καὶ τῶν συμμάχων οὐδένα προσλαβεῖν = it was not possible to admit anyone WITHOUT Philip and the allies (i.e. without their consent). The English 'apart from' reads as an exception (only Philip and the allies could be admitted), inverting the sense.
proposed_fix: saying that it was not possible to admit anyone without Philip and the allies

quote: They treated all the others of that party in the same way
problem: Greek: ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐχρήσαντο πᾶσι, 'they treated all the others alike', i.e. the other townspeople generally. 'Of that party' is not in the Greek and narrows the sense.
proposed_fix: They treated all the others in the same way

quote: The king then decided the whole matter
problem: Greek is ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς ἐπὶ πᾶσιν: the king spoke last of all (after the others), not that he decided everything; the parenthetical εἰ χρὴ τοῦ βασιλέως λέγειν τὰς τότε γνώμας and the later ἐπικυρωθείσης ... τῆς γνώμης show the opinion was still to be ratified.
proposed_fix: The king spoke last of all

quote: although they had many opportunities and favourable moments, they let them slip, and at times escaped from fears and dangers as well
problem: Greek: πολλὰς μὲν περιστάσεις καὶ καιροὺς ἔχοντες, ἐνίοτε δὲ φόβους καὶ κινδύνους διωλίσθανον. The περιστάσεις and καιροί are critical, dangerous junctures (parallel to φόβους καὶ κινδύνους), not opportunities; διολισθάνω means they slipped through/out of them. English reverses this into missed opportunities.
proposed_fix: although they often found themselves in critical straits and junctures, and at times in fears and dangers, they slipped through

quote: and they exchange these for grain, sometimes giving it when it is opportune, sometimes taking it
problem: σίτῳ δ᾽ ἀμείβονται, ποτὲ μὲν εὐκαίρως διδόντες, ποτὲ δὲ λαμβάνοντες: the Pontic peoples repay with grain, and the grain traffic runs both ways (sometimes giving, sometimes receiving). The English 'exchange these for grain' makes grain the one thing received, which contradicts 'sometimes giving it'.
proposed_fix: and in grain there is exchange in both directions, sometimes giving it when it suits, sometimes taking it

quote: opposite it, at a distance of nearly a thousand stades, there has formed a long bank, lying a day’s sail out from the shore
problem: σχεδὸν ἐπὶ χίλια στάδια συνεστάναι ταινίαν ἡμέρας δρόμον ἀπέχουσαν τῆς γῆς: the thousand stades is the LENGTH/extent of the bank (ἐπὶ χίλια στάδια), while its distance from land is a day's run. The English makes 1000 stades the distance from the Danube.
proposed_fix: toward it there has formed, over a stretch of nearly a thousand stades, a long bank lying a day’s sail out from the shore

quote: Such, then, was the war of the Rhodians against the Byzantines.
problem: The Greek stops mid-sentence: 'ὁ μὲν οὖν Ῥοδίων πρὸς Βυζαντίους πόλεμος' with the predicate ('διὰ ταῦτα καὶ τοιαύτην ἔλαβε τὴν ἀρχήν') only in the next chapter. The English closes the sentence as if whole (seam smoothed).
proposed_fix: Such, then, was the war of the Rhodians against the Byzantines—

quote: set about practically achieving their aim.
problem: The Greek breaks off mid-word: 'πρὸς τὸ καθικέσθαι τῆς προθέ' (προθέ[σεως] is a restoration). English completes it as 'their aim' without marking the cut.
proposed_fix: set about practically achieving their pur[...]

quote: and made their voyage back, as unexpectedly as they had come
problem: Greek: ῥίψαντες τὰ ὅπλα παναίσχρως, ἅμα δ᾽ ἀνελπίστως ἐποιήσατο τὸν ἀπόπλουν. ἀνελπίστως paired with παναίσχρως means in despair / without hope, not 'as unexpectedly as they had come'; the comparison with their arrival is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: and made their voyage back, in utter disgrace and without hope

quote: So this Olympiad year was drawing to a close.
problem: The Greek opens with only the tail of a sentence from the preceding (lost/cut) chapter: ὀλυμπιάδος. There is no verb and no 'year drawing to a close'; the English invents a complete sentence and smooths the break.
proposed_fix: [...] of the Olympiad.

quote: Pythias of Pallene
problem: Πυθίαν Πελληνέα: a man of Pellene (Achaean city), not Pallene (Chalcidic place).
proposed_fix: Pythias of Pellene

quote: Prolaus of Sicyon
problem: The Greek name is Πρόσλαον (accusative of Πρόσλαος), i.e. Proslaus, not Prolaus.
proposed_fix: Proslaus of Sicyon

quote: among them, the Eleans dwell exceptionally well off
problem: Greek is a fragment: [...]νόντων, οἰκοῦσι διαφερόντως Ἠλεῖοι = 'the Eleans inhabit [the country] especially/above all'. Nothing in the Greek corresponds to 'well off'; it is invented, and 'among them' is supplied to cover the gap. The text before the break is lost (lacuna), so the exact sense of what they inhabit is unrecoverable.
proposed_fix: among them [...], the Eleans especially make their homes

quote: but after whom Fortune turned against them
problem: Greek: ἕως τῆς ἐν Λεύκτροις μάχης, αὖτις ἐπὶ τἀναντία τραπείσης αὐτοῖς τῆς τύχης = 'down to the battle of Leuctra, after which Fortune turned to the opposite for them'. 'after whom' wrongly makes a person the antecedent; it is the time/battle of Leuctra.
proposed_fix: but then Fortune turned against them

quote: provide three months’ pay for the army, and add ten thousand measures of grain.
problem: Greek: πεντήκοντα τάλαντα ... αὐτῷ δοῦσι παραχρῆμα τριμήνου μισθοδοτῆσαι τὴν δύναμιν καὶ σίτου προσθεῖναι μυριάδας. The fifty talents are the means of paying the army three months (δοῦσι ... μισθοδοτῆσαι), not a separate item; and μυριάδας stands with no numeral (a number has dropped out or been lost), so 'ten thousand' is supplied, not read.
proposed_fix: pay the army three months’ wages with it, and add myriads [numeral missing in the Greek] of grain.

quote: At this time Aristophanes the general arrived
problem: Greek: Ἀριστόφαντος ὁ στρατηγός, i.e. Aristophantus (the Acarnanian strategos), not Aristophanes.
proposed_fix: At this time Aristophantus the general arrived

quote: they gave orders to carry off the most valuable furnishings and whatever could be transported
problem: Greek: τῆς μὲν κατασκευῆς τὰ πολυτελέστατα καὶ τὰ δυνατὰ κομίζεσθαι διέλεγον - they picked out/selected (διέλεγον) the most valuable furnishings, and those that could be carried; no order is given.
proposed_fix: they picked out the most valuable furnishings, and whatever could be carried, to take away

quote: they immediately fell upon it from the direction of Thermus and pressed hard on the last men in the column
problem: Greek: ἐπέβαλον εὐθέως εἰς τὸν Θέρμον καὶ προσέκειντο τοῖς ἐσχάτοις - they immediately burst into/occupied Thermus (which Philip's rear had just left) and pressed on the rearmost; not an attack coming from Thermus.
proposed_fix: they immediately burst into Thermus and pressed hard on the last men in the column

quote: the affair of the people of Palairos
problem: Greek has τὸν περὶ τοὺς Παλαιεῖς ἐμποδισμόν: the Paleis, people of Pale in Cephallenia (the same Paleis besieged by Philip, as ch. 17 has it), not Palairos in Acarnania (which would be Παλαιρεῖς).
proposed_fix: the affair of the people of Pale

quote: crossed the gulf, and came to anchor at Leucas as quickly as possible. There he instructed the officers
problem: Greek has ὡς θᾶττον εἰς τὴν Λευκάδα καθωρμίσθη, τοῖς … συνέταξε: temporal 'as soon as he had anchored at Leucas, he instructed ...', not 'anchored as quickly as possible'.
proposed_fix: crossed the gulf, and as soon as he had anchored at Leucas he instructed the officers

quote: at most two stades from the city
problem: τόπος ἀπέχων μὲν τῆς πόλεως δύο μάλιστα σταδίους: μάλιστα with a number means 'about', not 'at most'.
proposed_fix: about two stades from the city

quote: As the day was already drawing on
problem: ἤδη δὲ τῆς ὥρας συναγούσης: ὥρα here is the season of the year (the campaigning season closing, autumn), not the hour of the day.
proposed_fix: As the season was already drawing to a close

quote: promising that they would bring the Aetolians to agree to whatever was necessary for making peace
problem: ὑπισχνούμενοι πάντα ποιήσειν τοὺς Αἰτωλοὺς ἐφ᾽ ᾧ συνθέσθαι τὴν εἰρήνην: the Aetolians are the subject of ποιήσειν (the Aetolians would do everything to conclude peace), not the envoys bringing the Aetolians round.
proposed_fix: promising that the Aetolians would do everything required to conclude the peace

quote: The Aetolians, who had been hoping to exploit the situation in their own favor, were now eager to conclude peace
problem: Greek has only οἱ δ᾽ Αἰτωλοὶ τὰ μὲν ἔσπευδον ποιήσασθαι τὴν εἰρήνην (they were, on the one hand, eager for peace, pressed by the war); there is no clause about hoping to exploit the situation. The μὲν is answered by ἅμα δὲ ... παρεῖλκον below.
proposed_fix: The Aetolians, for their part, were eager to conclude peace

quote: withdrew, as ordered, to his quarters
problem: Greek reads ἀναχωρήσαντος εἰς ἱμάτιον... with a lacuna/corruption marker; εἰς ἱμάτιον ('into a cloak') is not 'quarters'. The English smooths a corrupt, gapped passage into a whole sentence.
proposed_fix: withdrew, as ordered, [text corrupt or lost here: Greek has εἰς ἱμάτιον ...]

quote: intending to launch his attack from higher ground on the right
problem: Greek ἐξ ὑπερδεξίου means from a commanding or advantageous (higher) position; it does not say 'on the right'. 'On the right' is added.
proposed_fix: intending to launch his attack from higher ground

quote: while farther north some parts of it look toward the Pontus in the region above the Phasis, and it stretches to the Hyrcanian Sea
problem: Greek: ὑπέρκειται δ᾽ αὐτῆς τινὰ μέρη τοῦ Πόντου κατὰ τοὺς ὑπὲρ τὸν Φᾶσιν τόπους; the subject is 'some parts of the Pontus', which lie above (beyond) Artabazanes' country. The English makes parts of his country look toward the Pontus.
proposed_fix: while above it lie some parts of the Pontus, in the region beyond the Phasis, and it adjoins the Hyrcanian Sea

quote: and second for warning him that his dealings with Ptolemy and, in general, his excessive agitation had not escaped notice
problem: The participles ἐγκαλῶν καὶ διαμαρτυρόμενος (reproaching, protesting) govern the first charge (ἐπὶ τῷ τετολμηκέναι διάδημα περιθέσθαι); the second item is δεύτερον δὲ προλέγων ὡς οὐ λανθάνει κοινοπραγῶν Πτολεμαίῳ, i.e. Antiochus himself WARNS (προλέγων) Achaeus that it is not unknown he is acting in concert with Ptolemy. The English makes Achaeus be reproached 'for warning him', inverting agent and sense.
proposed_fix: and second, warning him beforehand that it was not unknown to him that he was acting in concert with Ptolemy and, in general, was stirring more than was proper

quote: the city called Dura
problem: Greek has τὴν καλουμένην πόλιν Δῶρα, which is Dora (Dor on the Phoenician coast), not Dura.
proposed_fix: the city called Dora

quote: sixteen of his elephants died, but most of them were recaptured
problem: Greek: τῶν δ᾽ ἐλεφάντων ἑκκαίδεκα μὲν ἀπέθανον, ᾑρέθησαν δ᾽ αὐτῶν οἱ πλείους. ᾑρέθησαν = were captured (by the enemy); nothing says Ptolemy recovered them, and 'recaptured' reverses the sense (these are the losses on Ptolemy's side). The μὲν...δέ is a plain contrast of two losses, not a recovery.
proposed_fix: sixteen of his elephants died, and most of them were captured

quote: it was at this point that we broke off into our account of the Social War
problem: Greek: ἀπὸ γὰρ τούτων ἐποιησάμεθα τοῦ συμμαχικοῦ πολέμου τὴν ἐκτροπήν. ἐκτροπή is a turning aside/digression away from the Social War narrative; the English says he broke off 'into' it, which reverses the direction.
proposed_fix: it was at this point that we broke off our account of the Social War

quote: who were sailing in Taurion’s ships and had anchored alongside them as friends with four vessels
problem: Greek: Ἀγαθίνῳ δὲ καὶ Κασσάνδρῳ τοῖς Κορινθίοις ἐπιπλέουσι ταῖς Ταυρίωνος ναυσὶ ... μετὰ τεττάρων πλοίων. The Corinthians have their own four vessels (μετὰ τεττάρων πλοίων); ἐπιπλέουσι + dative means sailing up to / to join Taurion's ships, not sailing in them.
proposed_fix: who were sailing to join Taurion’s ships and had anchored alongside them as friends with four vessels

quote: —though the Romans approved of their conduct—they finally surrendered
problem: Greek: οὐδενὸς βοηθοῦντος, συνευδοκούντων Ῥωμαίων παρέδοσαν ἑαυτούς — the Romans consenting (genitive absolute), they surrendered. The Romans' consent was to the surrender; the English makes it a concessive 'though' about their conduct.
proposed_fix: , they finally surrendered with the Romans’ consent

quote: But Hieronymus, already leaning strongly toward the Carthaginians, said
problem: Greek: ὁ δ᾽ Ἱερώνυμος ἔτ᾽ ἐγγὺς ἐπόντων τῶν πρεσβευτῶν [εἴτ᾽ ἐν μισειόντων] τῶν Καρχηδονίων — the text is corrupt (editor's bracket) but the sense is that the Carthaginian envoys were still at hand/present; nothing says he was 'leaning' toward them. The English smooths a corrupt passage into an invented statement.
proposed_fix: But Hieronymus, while the Carthaginian envoys were still at hand (the Greek here is corrupt), said

quote: whom all the Siceliots alone had willingly and deliberately approved as their leader and king
problem: Greek: ὃν μόνον κατὰ προαίρεσιν καὶ κατ᾽ εὔνοιαν Σικελιῶται πάντες εὐδόκησαν σφῶν αὐτῶν ἡγεμόν᾽ εἶναι καὶ βασιλέα — μόνον agrees with ὃν (Pyrrhus): he was the only man whom all the Siceliots willingly approved. The English attaches 'alone' to the Siceliots.
proposed_fix: the only man whom all the Siceliots had willingly and deliberately approved as their leader and king

quote: and likewise of the Epirotes, Acarnanians, and all the others to whom in a short time he became the cause of many benefits.
problem: The Greek reads 'ἅμα δὲ τούτοις Ἠπειρωτῶν, Ἀκαρνάνων,... ὅσων ἑκάστοις ἀγαθῶν ἐν βραχεῖ χρόνῳ παραίτιος ἐγένετο': there is a gap after Ἀκαρνάνων, and the clause 'ὅσων ... ἀγαθῶν' is an indirect exclamation ('how many benefits to each'). The English invents 'and all the others' and reads on as if the sentence were whole; the lacuna is smoothed over.
proposed_fix: and likewise of the Epirotes and Acarnanians [...] and of how many benefits he was in a short time the cause to each of them.

quote: Therefore the soldiers there stood speechless, amazed by the strangeness of the thing and at the same time, as they foresaw and feared what would happen, filled alike with dread and delight.
problem: Greek: 'οἱ μὲν ἐκπεπληγμένοι τὸ παράδοξον, οἱ δὲ προορώμενοι καὶ δεδιότες τὸ συμβησόμενον, ἀχανεῖς ἅμα δὲ περιχαρεῖς ὄντες, ἕστασαν'. The οἱ μὲν ... οἱ δὲ contrast divides the men into two groups (some struck by the strangeness, others foreseeing and fearing the outcome); the English merges them into one group feeling both.
proposed_fix: Therefore some stood struck by the strangeness of the thing, and others foresaw and feared what would happen, all of them alike speechless and overjoyed.

quote: but were disputing over Sardinia and Sicily as well, and were trying to grasp everything
problem: Greek has a marked gap: ἠμφισβήτουν:... καὶ πάντα περιελάμβανον. The English reads straight on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: but were disputing over Sardinia and Sicily as well [text lost here] ... and were trying to grasp everything

quote: watching from within the city his own assaults beaten off with loss to himself and laughter from the defenders
problem: Greek: θεωρῶν μετὰ βλάβης καὶ χλευασμοῦ τοὺς ἔνδον ἀποτριβομένους αὑτοῦ τὰς ἐπιβολάς. τοὺς ἔνδον are the men inside (the defenders), who are warding off his plans. Marcus is not within the city.
proposed_fix: seeing the men inside parry his attempts, to his own loss and mockery

quote: Archimedes was ladling the sea out of his ships
problem: Greek: ταῖς μὲν ναυσὶν αὐτοῦ κυαθίζειν ἐκ θαλάττης Ἀρχιμήδη. Archimedes uses Marcus's ships as ladles (κύαθοι) to draw water from the sea. The English reverses this by making the ships the source the sea is ladled out of.
proposed_fix: Archimedes was using his ships as ladles to dip water out of the sea

quote: Demetrius, after rashly and recklessly attempting
problem: Greek opens with a fragment and a gap: καταλαβέσθαι... ἐγχειρήσας. No subject is preserved in the text; Demetrius comes only from the editor's footnote (cf. Polyb. III 19, 11). The English presents it as a complete sentence with a stated subject.
proposed_fix: [Demetrius (name supplied by the editor; the opening of the sentence is lost)] ... having rashly and recklessly attempted

quote: whereas someone already occupied with a royal court, if chance and opportunity offered, might perhaps shift to the greater and more illustrious name of Greece.
problem: Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ προκαταληφθεὶς ὑπὸ βασιλικῆς δυναστείας, καὶ τυχὼν ἐξουσίας, οὐδεὶς ἂν ἐπέσχε σὺν καιρῷ ποιήσασθαι μετάβασιν ἐπὶ τὸ τῆς Ἑλλάδος ὄνομα καὶ πρόσωπον. This is a negated universal (οὐδὲ ... οὐδεὶς ἂν ἐπέσχε: no one, once held by royal power and given the chance, would hold back from the timely change to the name and face of Greece), not a mere possibility ('might perhaps shift'). The English also drops the qualifier ἀκεραίῳ χρώμενος γνώμῃ (with a sound mind) from the preceding clause.
proposed_fix: whereas no one already held by royal power, given the opportunity, would hold back from making the timely change to the name and face of Greece.

quote: a place not open to siege-works but held secure by the continuous presence of Cambylus
problem: Greek: τι τῶν φυλακτηρίων τῶν κατὰ τοὺς ὄπισθε τόπους τῆς ἄκρας, οἵτινες κατασκευὴν μὲν οὐκ ἐπεδέχοντο, τῇ δὲ συνεχείᾳ τῶν ὑπὸ τὸν Καμβύλον τεταγμένων ἀνδρῶν ἐτηροῦντο. κατασκευή is construction or fortification of the posts themselves: these posts did not admit of fortification (the ground did not allow it), and were instead kept secure by the constant presence of Cambylus' men. 'Siege-works' (works by an attacker) misreads the sense.
proposed_fix: which did not admit of fortification but were guarded by the continuous presence of Cambylus

quote: Delighted at first, he promised everything; but then, in some distrust, he examined in detail the several plans and preparations.
problem: τὰ μὲν ὑπερχαρὴς ὢν πάνθ᾽ ὑπισχνεῖτο, τὰ δὲ διαπιστῶν ἐξήταζε: τὰ μὲν ... τὰ δὲ means 'in part ... in part', two simultaneous attitudes, not a sequence 'at first ... but then'. The true sequence comes only with μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα πιστεύσας in the next sentence.
proposed_fix: Partly overjoyed, he promised everything; partly distrustful, he examined in detail the several plans and preparations.

quote: afterward to make his move, by a circuitous route, toward Syria
problem: μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ποιήσασθαι δίχα προόδου τὴν ὁρμὴν ἐπὶ τοὺς κατὰ Συρίαν τόπους: δίχα προόδου is 'without any preliminary advance' (a sudden dash); nothing in the Greek says 'circuitous route'.
proposed_fix: afterward to make his dash, without any preliminary advance, for the regions of Syria

quote: led him by the same route by which he had come, and brought him alone before Antiochus
problem: ᾗ μὲν ἦλθε νυκτί, ταύτῃ παράγει πρὸς τὸν Ἀντίοχον τὸν Βῶλιν ὁ Καμβύλος μόνος πρὸς μόνον: ᾗ ... νυκτί is dative of time, 'on the night on which he came, on that same night'; there is no 'route'. μόνος πρὸς μόνον: Cambylus, alone, to the king, alone (private audience).
proposed_fix: brought him, on that same night, to Antiochus, in private, with no one else present

quote: the task would be difficult for those in whom he trusted
problem: δύσχρηστος ἡ πρόθεσις ἀπέβαινε τοῖς πεπιστευμένοις: οἱ πεπιστευμένοι are those entrusted with the task (Bolis and Cambylus), not men in whom Achaeus (or anyone) put trust; 'he' invites misreading as Achaeus.
proposed_fix: the task would be difficult for those entrusted with it

quote: some joining Ariobazus and others Laodice
problem: Greek reads οἱ μὲν πρὸς Ἀρίβαζον: the name is Aribazus (Ἀρίβαζος), not Ariobazus/Ariobarzanes.
proposed_fix: some joining Aribazus and others Laodice

quote: acting on the expectation fostered by the young men
problem: Greek: κατὰ τὴν τῶν νεανίσκων πρόληψιν = in accordance with the young men's anticipation (they had foreseen and planned that he would spend the day in the Museum, cf. 8.25 ταύτην ἐτάξαντο τὴν ἡμέραν). The expectation is the young men's, not one fostered in Livius.
proposed_fix: just as the young men had anticipated

quote: it was impossible for so many horsemen and so many pack animals to bring hay and barley on their backs from a great distance
problem: Greek: τοῖς δὲ νώτοις οὐκ ἐφικτὸν εἶναι τοσαύτῃ μὲν ἵππῳ, τοσούτοις δ᾽ ὑποζυγίοις κατανύσαι χόρτον ἢ κριθὰς κομίζοντας ἐκ μακροῦ διαστήματος. The cavalry and pack animals (datives) are the consumers to be supplied; the carrying is done by the transport (on backs) from far away. English makes the horsemen and pack animals the carriers.
proposed_fix: it was impossible, by carrying hay or barley on their backs from a great distance, to supply so large a body of cavalry and so many pack animals

quote: since even apart from the cavalry the danger of an evenly matched engagement seemed uncertain enough
problem: Greek: πρὸς οὓς καὶ τὸν ἐξ ἴσου κίνδυνον αὐτοῖς ἀμφίδοξον εἶναι συνέβαινε χωρὶς τῶν ἱππέων. 'Without the cavalry' (the Carthaginians would be encamped without it): even a fight on equal terms was doubtful for them. 'Even apart from the cavalry' can read as setting the cavalry aside, which blurs the point.
proposed_fix: since, without their cavalry, even a fight on equal terms was of doubtful issue for them

quote: they may become eager to imitate them.
problem: The Greek has a gap (`*`) right after ζηλωταὶ γίνωνται, before παράβολον ἔχειν τι καὶ κινδυνῶδες. The sentence beginning τὸ ... παράβολον ἔχειν lost its governing words, and the English reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: they may become eager to imitate them [...]

quote: it is clear that the sign lying opposite it must be the one rising.
problem: The Greek reads δῆλον ὡς δύναντος τούτου τὴν κατὰ διάμετρον ἐπιτέλλειν ἀνάγκη: the diametrically opposite sign must rise when the sun sets. The English drops the genitive absolute δύναντος τούτου (when the sun sets).
proposed_fix: it is clear that, when the sun sets, the sign diametrically opposite it must rise.

quote: wait there quietly with his force
problem: Greek reads 'ὡς ἐπὶ * πρεπίου μένειν ἐνσχολάσαντα μετὰ τῆς δυνάμεως': there is a gap/corruption marked * before 'πρεπίου', and nothing in the Greek means 'quietly' (ἐνσχολάσαντα = spending time/lingering). The English smooths the gap away.
proposed_fix: wait with his force, passing the time [Greek text defective here: 'as if for … prepion']

quote: left no city untouched by the name and reality of slavery
problem: Greek: 'οὐδεμίαν πόλιν ἄμοιρον ἐποίησαν τοῦ τῆς δουλείας ὀνόματος' - only 'the name of slavery'; 'and reality' is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: left no city without a share in the name of slavery

quote: For the Aetolians alone among the Greeks stood face to face with Antipater
problem: The Greek of the preceding sentence ends in an ellipsis ('παρασπόνδησις...') and this sentence begins with 'γάρ', so a gap in the source precedes it; the English reads on as if continuous.
proposed_fix: [Greek text lost here.] For the Aetolians alone among the Greeks stood face to face with Antipater

quote: set about piratical violence at sea and seized Pylus in violation of treaty
problem: Greek: κατὰ μὲν θάλατταν βιάζεσθαι καὶ παρασπονδεῖν ἐπεβάλοντο Πύλον. ἐπεβάλοντο is 'they undertook/attempted', governing the infinitives and Πύλον; it does not say Pylus was taken. 'Piratical' is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: set about attacking Pylus by sea, by force and in breach of treaty

quote: because alone among the Greeks they had resolved to remain quiet during the Persian invasion
problem: Greek: Θηβαίους τοὺς κατ᾽ ἀνάγκην ἡσυχίαν ἄγειν βουλευσαμένους μόνους τῶν Ἑλλήνων; the Thebans resolved to keep quiet 'under compulsion' (κατ᾽ ἀνάγκην); the English omits this qualifier, making the neutrality look wholly voluntary.
proposed_fix: because alone among the Greeks they had resolved, under compulsion, to remain quiet during the Persian invasion

quote: the Aeginetans who had not escaped gathered by the ships
problem: Greek: ὅσοι μὴ διεκλάπησαν; διακλέπτω means to be stolen away / made away with (privately carried off by soldiers), not 'to escape'. Those gathered are those who had not been spirited away.
proposed_fix: the Aeginetans who had not been stolen away gathered by the ships

quote: the boats were heavily loaded
problem: Greek: ἅτε καταγόμων μὲν ὄντων τῶν πλοίων; the boats were being brought down (downstream); nothing about heavy loading.
proposed_fix: the boats were being brought downstream

quote: Arsinoe is a city of Libya. Its ethnic is Arsinoites
problem: Greek has a lacuna marker (... τὸ ἐθνικὸν Ἀρσινοΐτης) between the Libyan Arsinoe entry and the ethnic; the English joins them as a continuous statement ('Its ethnic'), smoothing the gap.
proposed_fix: Arsinoe is a city of Libya. [...] The ethnic is Arsinoites

quote: And so, by abusing the freedom he enjoyed while staying among them, he deeply offended many of the Achaeans, and especially the respectable men among them.
problem: Greek reads διὸ καὶ χρώμενος τῇ κατὰ τὴν παρεπιδημίαν ἐξουσίᾳ *** ἀνέδην πολλοὺς ἐλύπει τῶν Ἀχαιῶν: there is a lacuna (***) after ἐξουσίᾳ that the English smooths over; 'abusing' and 'deeply' are not in the Greek (χρώμενος = using; ἀνέδην = without restraint).
proposed_fix: And so, using the authority he held during his stay among them [lacuna in the Greek], he distressed many of the Achaeans without restraint, and especially the respectable men among them.

quote: Claudius’ son, though wounded, only barely and unexpectedly escaped the danger.
problem: Greek ends with an accusative object clause (καὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Κλαυδίου τραυματίαν, μόλις καὶ παραδόξως τὸν κίνδυνον διαπεφευγότα) followed by a lacuna marker ***; the governing verb is lost. English supplies a finite verb and closes the sentence as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: As for Claudius’ son, wounded, who had barely and unexpectedly escaped the danger, [gap in the text]

quote: Once both torches are visible, the outlets are to be opened immediately.
problem: Greek: γενομένων δὲ φανερῶν ἀμφοτέρων ἅμα τῶν πυρσῶν καθελεῖν. εἶτ᾽ εὐθέως ἀφεῖναι τοὺς αὐλίσκους ῥεῖν. The lowering of the torches (καθελεῖν) is a separate step before the outlets are opened; the English omits it.
proposed_fix: Once both torches are visible at the same time, they are to be lowered, and then the outlets are to be opened at once.

quote: And that is why properly organized history is supremely useful in this matter too.
problem: Greek: διὸ καὶ τοῦτο γίνεται τῆς δεόντως ἱστορίας συντεταγμένης ὠφελιμώτατον. The subject is τοῦτο (this very part/digression), which becomes the most useful element of a duly composed history (partitive genitive); the English makes history itself the subject and loses the superlative's partitive sense.
proposed_fix: And that is why this too proves the most useful part of a properly composed history.

quote: In this engagement the king’s horse was killed after being wounded,
problem: Greek has two lacunae: τὸν μὲν ἵππον συμβαίνει *** ἀποθανεῖν τραυματισθέντα ***. The English reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: In this engagement it happened that the horse [text missing] was killed, having been wounded [text missing],

quote: because of the generals sent out from Carthage to Iberia
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: 'διὰ τὸ *** τοὺς ἐπαποστελλομένους ἐκ Καρχηδόνος εἰς Ἰβηρίαν στρατηγούς'. A verb (infinitive after διὰ τὸ) is missing, so what the generals did or failed to do is lost. The English reads on as if the text were whole.
