proposed_fix: because [lacuna in the Greek] the generals sent out from Carthage to Iberia

quote: with courage worthy of the son of Barca
problem: Greek 'ἀξίως μὲν τοῦ πατρὸς Βάρκα' = worthily of his father Barca (Hamilcar). The English makes the standard the 'son of Barca', which misidentifies who is the model.
proposed_fix: worthily of his father Barca

quote: could no longer even remain in Italy
problem: Greek 'τότε μηδ᾽ ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ νομίζειν παρεῖναι' = they thought he was not even present in Italy. The English turns this into a modal claim that he could not remain.
proposed_fix: was not even in Italy

quote: Yet another declared
problem: Greek 'ὁ δὲ' is a definite singular subject ('but he'), not 'another'. The antecedent is lost in the excerpt (likely Hannibal, the last person named), so the identity is uncertain; 'another' is unwarranted.
proposed_fix: But he declared

quote: but if not, they were to call the gods and the ambassadors then present from the other Greek states to witness
problem: Greek has a lacuna: 'ἑτοίμως δέχεσθαι *** τοὺς θεοὺς καὶ τοὺς πρεσβευτὰς ... ἐπιμαρτυραμένους χωρίζεσθαι'. The alternative clause ('but if not') is not in the Greek; it is supplied by the translator, smoothing the gap.
proposed_fix: [lacuna in the Greek] they were to call the gods and the ambassadors then present from the other Greek states to witness

quote: had very nearly failed to get Attalus into his hands
problem: Greek 'παρὰ μικρὸν ἔλθοι τοῦ λαβεῖν τὸν Ἄτταλον ὑποχείριον' = he came within a little of capturing Attalus (and missed him). The English 'nearly failed to get' implies he almost missed but did get him, inverting the sense of the lament.
proposed_fix: had come very close to getting Attalus into his hands

quote: showing bad judgment in the former case and bad temper in the latter
problem: Greek 'κακῶς μὲν πρὸ τοῦ, κακῶς δὲ τότε χρώμενος τῷ θυμῷ' = using his temper badly before and badly then. The same fault (θυμός) is meant on both occasions; the English invents a contrast between judgment and temper.
proposed_fix: giving way to his temper badly before and badly now

quote: For although the citizens in democracies are generally more eager in military struggles than the civic subjects of tyrants, the mercenaries
problem: Greek has the proportional correlative ὅσῳ … τοσούτῳ ('by as much as … by so much'): the more eager the democratic masses are than the tyrants' civic subjects, the more the monarchs' mercenaries surpass those of democracies. English turns it into a concessive 'although'.
proposed_fix: For to the degree that the masses in democracies are more eager in military struggles than the citizens subject to tyrants, to that same degree the mercenaries

quote: when the entire mercenary force had broken the Achaeans and the left wing had collapsed
problem: τοῦ ξενικοῦ παντὸς ἐγκεκλικότος τοῖς Ἀχαιοῖς καὶ παραλελυμένου τοῦ λαιοῦ κέρως: the whole mercenary force of the Achaeans had given way and the left wing was broken up. English inverts the agent (mercenaries broke the Achaeans).
proposed_fix: when the entire Achaean mercenary force had given way and the left wing had been broken up

quote: he neither fled in panic nor withdrew in despair.
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) after ἀπέστη, before ἀλλ᾽ ὑποστείλας; English reads on as if whole.
proposed_fix: he neither fled in panic nor withdrew in despair [gap in the Greek text here].

quote: he immediately ordered the front companies of the phalanx to wheel with locked shields and advance at the double
problem: εὐθέως τοῖς πρώτοις τέλεσι … ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδα κλίνων, προῆγε μετὰ δρόμου: Philopoemen himself wheeled the leading companies to the left (ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδα = toward the shield side) and advanced at a run; 'locked shields' is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: he immediately wheeled the front companies of the phalanx to the left and advanced at the double

quote: Polybius the Megalopolitan to gather the remaining Illyrians, armored troops, and mercenaries who had not joined in the flight
problem: Πολυαίνῳ δ᾽ ἐπέταξε τῷ Μεγαλοπολίτῃ: the man is Polyaenus, not Polybius. Also τοὺς διακεκλικότας τὴν φυγήν = those who had turned/scattered in flight, the opposite of 'had not joined in the flight'.
proposed_fix: Polyaenus the Megalopolitan to gather the survivors and the Illyrians, armored troops, and mercenaries who had scattered in flight

quote: found himself beyond the enemy’s wing
problem: ὑπερδέξιος τοῦ τῶν πολεμίων κέρατος means in a commanding position above/over the enemy's wing, not 'beyond' it.
proposed_fix: found himself in a commanding position over the enemy’s wing

quote: In just such situations it is the commanders who are most often exposed to the gravest danger.
problem: Greek ends in a lacuna: ἐν οἷς δὴ καὶ μέγιστα συμβαίνει τοὺς ἡγουμένους *** ; the predicate is missing. English invents a complete sentence.
proposed_fix: In just such situations it very often happens that the commanders [text breaks off here in the Greek].

quote: Masannasan with the Numidians
problem: Greek has Μασαννάσαν (accusative of Μασαννάσας, i.e. Masinissa); the English reproduces the Greek accusative ending as if it were part of the name.
proposed_fix: Masinissa with the Numidians

quote: he ordered the Iberians to keep advancing in the same formation.
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) after τὴν ἐπαγωγήν and then breaks off mid-sentence (τῷ μὲν δεξιῷ τὰς σημαίας καὶ τὰς ἴλας ἐπι-). The English reads as a complete sentence and hides both the gap and the truncation.
proposed_fix: he ordered the Iberians to keep their ranks and make their advance in the same way [gap in the Greek text] ... the right wing, the standards and squadrons ... [the text breaks off here].

quote: divided them behind the battle line between the two wings
problem: Greek μερίσας ἐφ᾽ ἑκάτερον κέρας ὀπίσω τῶν παρατεταγμένων: he divided them to each wing, behind the line; not placed between the wings.
proposed_fix: divided them, one part to each wing, behind the battle line

quote: and within each wing the infantry of the cavalry
problem: Greek καὶ καθόλου τὸ δεξιὸν κέρας τῷ λαιῷ καὶ κατὰ μέρος οἱ πεζοὶ τοῖς ἱππεῦσιν: in general the right wing was the reverse of the left, and in particular the infantry the reverse of the cavalry. English leaves 'the infantry of the cavalry', which loses the contrast.
proposed_fix: and, in detail, the infantry's movement was the reverse of the cavalry's

quote: When the tribunes had explained what had been decided
problem: Greek has an explicit lacuna marker (...) between the first sentence (περὶ τὴν τῶν χρημάτων ἐπιμέλειαν) and τῶν δὲ χιλιάρχων διασαφούντων. English joins them seamlessly.
proposed_fix: [gap in the Greek text] When the tribunes had explained what had been decided

quote: prepare rations for a longer expedition within three days
problem: Greek πρὸ ἡμερῶν τριῶν ἐφόδια παρεσκευάσθαι κατὰ πλείω χρόνον: provisions to be ready three days beforehand, for a longer time. 'Within three days' is not what πρὸ ἡμερῶν τριῶν says; the phrase is somewhat compressed.
proposed_fix: have provisions prepared three days in advance, for a longer period

quote: after this first movement, they should lay down the baggage
problem: The Greek has a lacuna (***) in 'ὅταν ἐκπορευομένοις *** μετὰ τοῦτο τὸ πρῶτον τὰς μὲν ἀποσκευὰς ἀποτιθέναι'; the English reads on as if the clause were whole and supplies a smooth sense for the damaged words.
proposed_fix: [gap in the Greek text here] ... first of all, they should lay down the baggage

quote: were brought in naked and in chains
problem: The Greek has a lacuna after 'δεδεμένοι γυμνοὶ ***' before 'οἱ τῆς στάσεως αἰτίαι γεγονότες εἰσήγοντο'; the English presents the sentence as complete.
proposed_fix: were brought in bound and naked [gap in the Greek text here]

quote: he drew up a counterforce against the enemy stationed on the foothills
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: 'ἀντέταττε *** πρὸς δὲ τοὺς εἰς τὸν αὐλῶνα καταβεβηκότας'. The object of ἀντέταττε (what he set against the foothill troops) is missing; 'a counterforce' is invented to smooth the gap.
proposed_fix: he drew up [gap in the Greek text here: the troops he set] against the enemy stationed on the foothills

quote: especially along the coast, among the Etruscans and the Gauls
problem: The Greek reads καὶ μάλιστα [τὴν παλαίαν], παρά τε τοῖς Τυρρηνικοῖς καὶ Γαλάταις. The words τὴν παλαίαν ('the old') are bracketed in the edition as doubtful or corrupt. 'Along the coast' is not in the Greek and silently smooths over the corrupt words.
proposed_fix: especially among the Etruscans and the Gauls

quote: but rather what it befits themselves to do—so too with abuse
problem: The Greek breaks off at 'τοῦτο μᾶλλον *' and resumes after a gap at '** οὕτως καὶ περὶ τῶν λοιδοριῶν'. The English runs the two halves together as one whole sentence, silently smoothing the lacuna.
proposed_fix: but rather what it befits themselves to do, this more [...] [text lost] ... so too with abuse

quote: even if some such disgrace had truly attached to Demochares
problem: ἀτύχημα means 'misfortune, mishap', not 'disgrace'.
proposed_fix: even if some such misfortune had truly attached to Demochares

quote: not realizing that falsehood is no less present in those who in their histories pass over in silence what actually happened than in those who misstate it
problem: Greek has a lacuna: 'τοὺς τὰ γεγονότα *** γράφοντας ἐν ταῖς ἱστορίαις' (falsehood is no less found among those who write the events [gap] in their histories). The English invents a complete contrast (silence vs misstatement) that the surviving Greek does not give.
proposed_fix: not realizing that falsehood is no less found among those who write what happened [text lost] in their histories

quote: offering his backside to the front of all who wished
problem: 'πάντων τῶν βουλομένων τοῖς ὄπισθεν ἔμπροσθεν γεγονότα': he became, for all who wished, 'front' to their 'behind' (his front put in the place of the rear). The English reverses who offers what and garbles the reversal-of-front-and-back point.
proposed_fix: having made his front a rear for all who wished

quote: the Aetolians had slipped into debt without realizing it themselves, much less anyone else.
problem: ἔλαθον οὐ μόνον ἄλλους, ἀλλὰ καὶ σφᾶς αὐτούς: they escaped notice not only of others but even of themselves. The English reverses the climax ('much less anyone else').
proposed_fix: the Aetolians had fallen deeply into debt without it being noticed, not only by others but even by themselves.

quote: This was the kind of villainy that followed
problem: ἐγένετο περὶ τὴν τοιαύτην κακοπραγμοσύνην: 'was engaged in / occupied with such villainy'. The subject is not in the extract (fragment begins mid-sentence, presumably Philip); the English invents a sequential 'that followed' and smooths the missing subject.
proposed_fix: [...] was engaged in this kind of villainy

quote: For Philip wished above all either to manage the whole business himself or at least to keep his intentions in these matters from becoming apparent to the Rhodians.
problem: πᾶν γὰρ βουληθῆναι τὸν Φίλιππον ἀναδέξασθαι ἢ καταφανῆ γενέσθαι Ῥοδίοις τὴν ἐν τούτοις αὐτοῦ προαίρεσιν: Philip was willing to take on/undergo anything rather than let his intention in these matters become apparent to the Rhodians. The English invents 'manage the business himself' and turns 'rather than' into 'either...or'.
proposed_fix: For Philip was willing to take on anything rather than let his intentions in these matters become apparent to the Rhodians.

quote: After greeting the man, the figure, once he had raised the woman from her seat and embraced her with his arms, would gradually draw him toward her breasts.
problem: καὶ δεξιωσάμενος, ἐπειδὰν ἐκ τῆς καθέδρας ἀνέστησε τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ περιέπτυξε ταῖς χερσί, προσήγετο κατὰ βραχὺ πρὸς τὰ στέρνα: Nabis greets the man, raises the 'woman' (the figure) from her seat, and (she) embraces/is made to embrace the man, then he is drawn gradually to her chest. The English makes the figure the subject, has 'he' raise 'the woman' as if she were a separate person, and makes the woman the one embraced. The object of περιέπτυξε is unexpressed, so who embraces whom is slightly ambiguous, but it is the victim who is drawn to the breast.
proposed_fix: After greeting the man, Nabis would raise the figure from its seat, have it put its arms around him, and gradually draw him toward its breast.

quote: because of the prosperity of the Gerrhaeans
problem: διὰ τὴν εὐκαιρίαν τῶν Γερραίων: εὐκαιρία is convenience/advantage (of suitability or opportunity), not prosperity; the land is fitted out with villages and towers 'for the convenience of the Gerrhaeans', who occupy it.
proposed_fix: for the convenience of the Gerrhaeans

quote: even if they gladly follow each separate action and speech in detail
problem: Greek: κἂν ὁλοσχερῶς παραδέχωνται τὰ κατὰ μέρος ἔργα καὶ λόγους. ὁλοσχερῶς means broadly/in outline (opposed to κατὰ μέρος, in particulars); there is no 'gladly' and no following 'in detail'. The sense is that people may take in the particular deeds and speeches only in general terms, yet still long to know the end.
proposed_fix: even if they take in the particular actions and speeches only in outline

quote: this seems to me the finest and boldest of all his achievements.
problem: The Greek ends with a lacuna marker: κάλλιστον εἶναί μοι δοκεῖ τοῦτο τοὔργον καὶ παραβολώτατον τῶν ἐκείνῳ πεπραγμένων ***. The text breaks off after this clause; the English closes the sentence as if whole and does not mark the gap.
proposed_fix: this seems to me the finest and boldest of all his achievements [...]

quote: since a general with forces would very soon join him [...]
problem: Greek breaks off mid-clause: ὡς αὐτίκα μάλα τοῦ στρατηγοῦ μετὰ τῶν δυνάμεων (genitive with article, no verb preserved). English invents the missing predicate 'would join him' and turns 'the general' into 'a general'. Text is truncated; the verb and the identity of the general (probably Hasdrubal, just sent out, but not stated) are not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: since very soon the general, with his forces [...]

quote: they should omit no extreme measure in testing even this hope
problem: μηδεμίαν ὑπερβολὴν ποιησαμένους ἐξελέγχειν καὶ ταύτην τὴν ἐλπίδα: ὑπερβολή here means delay/postponement (ὑπερβολὴν ποιεῖσθαι), not an extreme measure; the sense is 'without any delay put even this hope to the test'.
proposed_fix: they should, without any delay, put even this hope to the test

quote: give him no time to recover his wits or prepare
problem: μὴ δοῦναι χρόνον εἰς ἐπίστασιν καὶ παρασκευήν: ἐπίστασις is halting/making a stand, not recovering wits.
proposed_fix: give him no time to make a stand or prepare

quote: for two years already
problem: Greek has δεύτερον ἔτος ἤδη φεύγοντες, 'already in the second year of flight', not 'two years already'.
proposed_fix: now in the second year

quote: had not merely appealed to the gods and kissed the ground, as men commonly do,
problem: Greek: τοὺς θεοὺς ἀσπάσαιντο (greeted/saluted the gods) and τὴν γῆν προσκυνήσαιεν (did obeisance to the earth), as other men customarily do. 'Appealed' and 'kissed the ground' are not what is said.
proposed_fix: had not merely greeted the gods and bowed down to the earth, as men commonly do,

quote: a friend of Syphax
problem: Greek has ὃς ἦν μὲν οἰκεῖος Σόφακος: οἰκεῖος means a relative or kinsman, not merely a friend.
proposed_fix: a kinsman of Syphax

quote: well suited in other respects and with a water supply close at hand.
problem: The Greek breaks off mid-sentence: πρός τε τἄλλα τόπον εὐφυῆ καταλαβόμενος καὶ τὴν … (text ends at 'and the'). 'A water supply close at hand' is not in the Greek given; the English silently completes a truncated sentence.
proposed_fix: well suited in other respects and ... [the Greek text breaks off here].

quote: And they did not, like tyrants, put forward even some small pretext to veil their shame
problem: Greek: οὐδ᾽ οὖν, καθάπερ οἱ τύραννοι, βραχεῖαν δή τινα προβαλλόμενοι τῆς αἰσχύνης πρόφασιν: 'not even, as tyrants do, putting forward some small pretext'. Tyrants do offer a pretext; these kings did not. The English makes tyrants the contrast, inverting the sense.
proposed_fix: And they did not, as even tyrants do, put forward some small pretext to veil their shame

quote: And in this matter Fortune plainly cooperated against Philip as well.
problem: Greek: καὶ γὰρ ἡ τύχη πρός γε τοῦτο τὸ μέρος αὐτῷ συνήργησε προφανῶς. συνεργεῖν + dative means 'cooperate with', and αὐτῷ is Philip; 'against' is not in the Greek, and καὶ γάρ is 'for indeed', not 'as well'. Polybius may intend irony (Fortune worked with him to expose him), but the Greek says 'with him'.
proposed_fix: For indeed, in this respect Fortune plainly cooperated with Philip.

quote: the Rhodians could hardly believe it because the faithlessness was so extreme
problem: Greek: μὴ δύνασθαι πιστεῦσαι διὰ τὴν ὑπερβολὴν τῆς ἀθεσίας. 'Were unable to believe', not 'could hardly believe' (which implies they did believe, barely).
proposed_fix: the Rhodians could not believe it, because of the extremity of the faithlessness

quote: All this happened before the negotiations with Philip, as I have said
problem: Greek: ταῦτα δ᾽ ἐγενήθη πρότερα τοῦ παρὰ Φιλίππῳ διαβουλίου ***, ὡς ἐδηλώσαμεν. There is a lacuna (***) after διαβουλίου that the English smooths over; also διαβούλιον is a deliberation or council held at Philip's court, not 'negotiations with Philip'.
proposed_fix: All this happened before the deliberation at Philip's court [...], as I have shown

quote: the knowledge that the coming struggle lay in their own hands, because they controlled all the supplies being brought into Alexandria
problem: Greek: γινώσκειν ὅτι τὸ μέλλειν καθ᾽ αὑτῶν ἐστι διὰ τὸ πάντων τῶν παρακομιζομένων ἐπιτηδείων ... κρατεῖν. τὸ μέλλειν is 'delay/hesitation' and καθ᾽ αὑτῶν 'against themselves' (the masses); the nearest possible subject of κρατεῖν is τῶν προεστώτων (those in power), so it is they who control the supplies, which is why delay hurts the masses. The English inverts this.
proposed_fix: the knowledge that delay told against themselves, because those in power controlled all the supplies being brought into Alexandria

quote: pitying the victims and regretting
problem: Greek: πρὸς πολλοὺς οἰκτιζόμενος καὶ μεταμελόμενος. οἰκτιζόμενος means 'lamenting/bewailing' (to many people); the Greek names no victims, and 'πρὸς πολλοὺς' (to many) is dropped, which is how it became known.
proposed_fix: lamenting to many people and regretting

quote: escaped half naked into a tent
problem: Greek says παρέπεσε γυμνὸς εἴς τινα σκηνήν: simply 'naked' (stripped), no 'half'; the English itself later says 'saw him naked' for ὁρῶντες αὐτὸν γυμνόν.
proposed_fix: escaped naked into a tent

quote: Moeragenes said that what was chiefly needed was only someone to take the lead.
problem: The sentence continues from ch. 28: ἀκμάζειν δὲ νῦν μάλιστα καὶ προσδεῖσθαι τῶν καταρξομένων. μάλιστα belongs with ἀκμάζειν (already rendered 'now in full strength'); the second clause is just 'and it wanted [only] those who would begin'. 'chiefly needed' misplaces μάλιστα.
proposed_fix: Moeragenes said that it also still needed people to make the start.

quote: convinced that if he could throw them into confusion he would then sail the rest of the way safely
problem: Greek: πεπεισμένος καταταχήσειν καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν ἀσφαλῶς ἤδη κομισθήσεσθαι. καταταχήσειν means he would get ahead of / outstrip them by speed; nothing about throwing the enemy into confusion.
proposed_fix: convinced that he would get the start of them and then sail the rest of the way safely

quote: besides undecked ships
problem: Greek: σὺν δὲ τούτοις ἄφρακτα *** — a number is missing after ἄφρακτα (lacuna); the English reads on as if whole.
proposed_fix: besides undecked ships [number lost in the Greek text]

quote: because the enemy vessel had a high-built prow
problem: Greek: ἀναστείρου τῆς νεὼς οὔσης — the genitive absolute does not name whose ship had the raised stem; the sense (he took the blow above the waterline) favors his own ship, the opposite of the English assignment. Ambiguous, so preserve the ambiguity.
proposed_fix: because the ship's stem was raised (the Greek does not say whose ship)

quote: but he struck the enemy below the waterline
problem: Greek: τὴν δὲ τῶν πολεμίων τρώσας ναῦν ὑπὸ τὰ * βίαχα — the text is corrupt/defective (asterisk, and βίαχα is not a known word); 'below the waterline' is an invented smoothing.
proposed_fix: but he struck the enemy ship under the [text corrupt: ὑπὸ τὰ * βίαχα]

quote: Philip had the advantage in the number of his light craft, but Attalus had the advantage in the number of decked ships.
problem: Greek: καθ᾽ ὅσον … ἐπλεόναζον οἱ παρὰ τοῦ Φιλίππου λέμβοι, κατὰ τοσοῦτον διέφερον οἱ περὶ τὸν Ἄτταλον τῷ τῶν καταφράκτων νεῶν πλήθει — a proportional correlative: by just as much as Philip's light boats were more numerous, by so much Attalus' side excelled in decked ships (the two balanced, hence ἐφάμιλλος). The English drops the correlation.
proposed_fix: For in proportion as Philip's light boats were more numerous, by just so much did Attalus' side excel in the number of decked ships.

quote: a gulf some call by one name and most call the Bargylian Gulf, after the cities built around its inner recess
problem: The Greek reads προσαγορευομένῳ ***, παρὰ δὲ τοῖς πλείστοις Βαργυλιητικῷ: the gulf's first name is lost in a lacuna (***). The English smooths the gap into 'some call by one name'. Greek says only that it is called [name lost], but by most the Bargylietic gulf, a name shared with the cities (συνωνύμως) at its head.
proposed_fix: a gulf called *** [name lost in the Greek] but by most the Bargylian Gulf, a name shared with the cities built around its inner recess

quote: never know how to stop opposing and resenting such declarations by historians throughout my whole work
problem: οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως ... ἐναντιούμενος καὶ δυσανασχετῶν διατελῶ: 'I do not know how it is, but I continually find myself opposing and resenting'. οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅπως is an idiom for 'somehow'; it does not mean 'I do not know how to stop'.
proposed_fix: somehow find myself, throughout my whole work, opposing and resenting such declarations by historians

quote: and become altogether deep and unfordable.
problem: The Greek ends the Alpheus passage with παντελῶς ἄβατος ὢν καὶ βαρύς. *** : a lacuna follows. The English reads on as if the passage were complete.
proposed_fix: and become altogether deep and unfordable. [Text lost here in the Greek.]

quote: seized the high ground on the right
problem: προκαταλαβόμενος τοὺς ὑπερδεξίους τόπους: 'having first occupied the commanding (overlooking) positions'. ὑπερδέξιος means advantageous high ground, not ground on the right; no side is stated (cf. ch. 18, τοὺς ὑπερκειμένους τῶν πολεμίων τόπους).
proposed_fix: seized the commanding ground

quote: naturally courageous
problem: Greek has a lacuna marked *** : 'στρατηγεῖν μὲν γὰρ ... δυνατὸς ἦν, καὶ *** ἀνδρώδης ὑπῆρχε τῇ φύσει'. The English reads on as if the clause were whole; the gap is smoothed over.
proposed_fix: [text missing] courageous by nature

quote: and increasingly contrasted him with Sosibius
problem: Greek: 'τὸν δὲ Σωσίβιον ἐκ παραθέσεως ἐθαύμαζον' - they ADMIRED Sosibius by comparison. The English drops the admiration (ἐθαύμαζον) and invents 'increasingly'; the next sentence (ἐδόκει γὰρ οὗτος ...) gives the grounds for the admiration.
proposed_fix: and by comparison admired Sosibius

quote: the people of Mylae, Alabanda, and Magnesia
problem: Greek 'Μυλασεῖς' = people of Mylasa in Caria (not Mylae, a Sicilian place).
proposed_fix: the people of Mylasa, Alabanda, and Magnesia

quote: against the city of Mylae
problem: Greek 'ἐπὶ τὴν Μυλασέων πόλιν' = the city of Mylasa.
proposed_fix: against the city of Mylasa

quote: For he was well aware of the embassies being sent to Rome against him, now that affairs in Libya had come to an end.
problem: Greek has a lacuna (* and ** ) after 'πρεσβείας εἰς Ῥώμην,' before 'διόπερ πέρας ἔχει τὰ κατὰ τὴν Λιβύην' ('therefore the affairs in Libya come to an end'). The English joins them as a seamless sentence and turns 'διόπερ' into a causal 'now that', smoothing the gap.
proposed_fix: For he was well aware of the embassies being sent to Rome against him, [text missing] ... hence the affairs in Libya were at an end.

quote: at times people even bridge it for those who wish to cross on foot between the continents, and at all times it is traversed by shipping
problem: Greek has ποτὲ μὲν γεφυρούμενον ... ποτὲ δὲ πλωτευόμενον συνεχῶς: at times bridged, at other times sailed across continuously. The μὲν...δέ contrast is lost; 'at all times' is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: at times it is bridged by those who choose to cross on foot to either continent, and at other times it is continuously crossed by ships

quote: and shattered the sarissas of others, then with the broken splinters stabbed their faces and exposed parts, throwing them into total confusion.
problem: Greek has a lacuna: ὧν δὲ συντρίβοντες τὰς σαρίσας αὐτοῖς τοῖς ἐκείνων κλάσμασιν ἐκ διαλήψεως *** τύπτοντες αὐτῶν ταῖς ἐπιδορατίσι τὰ πρόσωπα. The text breaks off after ἐκ διαλήψεως, and the English reads on as if whole. It also omits ταῖς ἐπιδορατίσι (spear-points/butt-spikes) and the force of ἐκ διαλήψεως.
proposed_fix: and breaking the sarissas of others, with the very fragments of them, [gap in the Greek text] striking their faces and exposed parts with the spear-points, they drove them into complete rout.

quote: the Jews living around the sanctuary of the place called Jerusalem also went over to him.
problem: Greek: οἱ περὶ τὸ ἱερὸν τὸ προσαγορευόμενον Ἱεροσόλυμα κατοικοῦντες. The participle προσαγορευόμενον (neuter singular) agrees with τὸ ἱερόν, so it is the sanctuary that is called Jerusalem, not a 'place' whose sanctuary it is. The following ὑπὲρ οὗ also refers back to the sanctuary.
proposed_fix: the Jews living around the sanctuary called Jerusalem also went over to him.

quote: the magnitude of the honors that had been bestowed on them by the Achaeans
problem: Greek: τὸ μέγεθος τῶν τιμῶν τῶν ἀπηντημένων αὐτοῖς παρὰ τῶν Ἀχαιῶν. The honors are those the Achaeans paid to the Macedonian kings (Antigonus and Philip), not to the Achaeans. In the English, 'them' follows 'conferred upon them by Antigonus' where 'them' = the Achaeans, so it reads as Achaeans honored by Achaeans. The Greek pronoun αὐτοῖς is itself loose, but the sense is fixed by context.
proposed_fix: the magnitude of the honors that the Achaeans had paid to Antigonus and to himself

quote: the Macedonians having already been twice defeated and most of their supplies on land used up
problem: Greek: τῶν τε Μακεδόνων προηττημένων δὶς ἤδη καὶ κατὰ γῆν πλείστων αὐτοῖς χορηγιῶν ἐκδεδαπανημένων. κατὰ γῆν most naturally goes with the twice-repeated defeat (twice already beaten, and on land), not with the supplies; πλείστων is a superlative of quantity (very great supplies/expenditures), not a proportion ('most of their supplies'). The English both misattaches the phrase and implies the stock was largely exhausted.
proposed_fix: the Macedonians having already been twice defeated, and on land, and very large supplies having been spent by them

quote: and they pick those that have these on one side only, not running off in every direction
problem: Greek has a lacuna here: καὶ ταύτας *** ἔχοντες λαμβάνονται * ** οὐκ ἐναλλάξ. The English fills the gap with 'on one side only' and reads on as if the text were whole; the transmitted words are only 'having these ... they are taken ... not alternately (οὐκ ἐναλλάξ)'.
proposed_fix: and having these [...] they are taken [...] not alternately [text lost in the Greek]

quote: sent off his rearguard
problem: τὴν δ᾽ ἐφεδρείαν ἀπέστειλε, συντάξας ἐπὶ τοὺς ἄκρους ἐπιβαλεῖν: the ἐφεδρεία is the covering/outpost force sent ahead to occupy the hill summits (called 'outpost' in chapters 21-22), not a rearguard.
proposed_fix: sent off his outpost force

quote: one part was locked in close combat with those fighting
problem: Greek has a lacuna: τὰ μὲν συνεχῆ τοῖς διαγωνιζομένοις ***, so the predicate is missing (only 'the part contiguous to those fighting ...'). The English supplies a verb and reads on as whole.
proposed_fix: one part, adjoining those fighting, [...] [text lost in the Greek]

quote: at first halted, since the enemy held their pikes upright
problem: The Greek has a lacuna: τὰς μὲν ἀρχὰς *** ἐπέστη, τῶν πολεμίων ὀρθὰς ἀνασχόντων τὰς σαρίσας. Text is missing after τὰς μὲν ἀρχὰς; the English reads on as if whole and supplies a causal 'since'.
proposed_fix: at first [...] halted, the enemy having held their pikes upright

quote: nor did he wish, having driven Philip from power, to leave the Aetolians as masters of the Greeks
problem: Greek is εἴτ᾽ οὐκ ἐβούλετο ... : εἴτε is disjunctive ('or whether he did not wish'), the second member of an alternative of motives, not a negative continuation ('nor'). The first member lies in the lacuna.
proposed_fix: or else he did not wish, having driven Philip from power, to leave the Aetolians as masters of the Greeks

quote: They tried to prevent Antiochus from sailing along the coast
problem: The Greek fragment opens with an ellipsis ('Res Asiae...') and then an infinitive clause, 'kolyein de ton Antiochon parapleein'; the finite subject and governing verb are lost. English supplies 'They tried' as if the sentence were whole (smoothed lacuna). The subject (who 'they' are) is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: [...] to prevent Antiochus from sailing along the coast

quote: And in their cleverness in arguing against one another, these speakers immediately gave themselves away.
problem: Greek: kai toutous eutheos epedeiknysan autoi kath' hauton dia tes pros allelous heuresilogias. 'toutous' (masc. acc.) refers to the places just mentioned (the retained ones of lesser appearance); the speakers themselves pointed out these very places, to their own detriment (kath' hauton), through their ingenuity in debating with one another. English drops the object and turns it into a vague 'gave themselves away'.
proposed_fix: And these very places they themselves immediately pointed out, to their own cost, through their ingenuity in arguing with one another.

quote: there also arrived two of the ten commissioners
problem: The Greek names three men: τῶν δέκα Πόπλιος μὲν Λέντλος ἐκ Βαργυλίων, Λεύκιος δὲ Τερέντιος καὶ Πόπλιος Οὐίλλιος ἐκ Θάσου (Lentulus, Terentius, Villius). 'Two' is a number error.
proposed_fix: there also arrived three of the ten commissioners

quote: The man who contributed most to this state of things was Opheltas, who was forever devising
problem: Greek has a lacuna: 'πλεῖστα δὲ συνεβάλετο πρὸς τὴν τοιαύτην *  ** Ὀφέλτας, αἰεί τι προσεπινοῶν' - text is missing after 'τοιαύτην' (the noun, and the subject's start) and before Ὀφέλτας. The English reads on as if whole and supplies a complete subject/predicate. The nominative Ὀφέλτας may be the subject or in apposition to a lost name; it is not certain Opheltas is the one who 'contributed most'.
proposed_fix: Most contributed to such a [gap in the Greek] ... Opheltas, who was forever devising

quote: during the long war against Nabis the Megalopolitans, being a neighboring people, had spent all that time serving under Philopoemen and had thus gained real training in military action
problem: Greek: τοῦ πρὸς Νάβιν πολέμου τοῖς Μεγαλοπολίταις ἀστυγείτονος ... πάντα τὸν χρόνον ὑπὸ τὸν Φιλοποίμενα τεταγμένος. ἀστυγείτονος (genitive singular) goes with Nabis/the war: Nabis was the neighbor of the Megalopolitans, not they the neighbor people; and the participle τεταγμένος is singular, so it is Diophanes who served under Philopoemen, not the Megalopolitans collectively.
proposed_fix: during the long war against Nabis, who was a neighbor of the Megalopolitans, he had spent all that time serving under Philopoemen and had thus gained real training in military action

quote: and reflecting that only by mastering the sea could he prevent the crossing of the land army and in general keep the war away from Asia, he resolved to fight a naval battle
problem: Greek has a lacuna marked *** : καὶ καθόλου τὸν πόλεμον ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀσίας ἀποτρίβεσθαι *** βεβαίως κρατοίη τῆς θαλάττης. The text breaks off after ἀποτρίβεσθαι and resumes mid-clause with 'if/so that he might securely command the sea'; the English reads on as if the sentence were whole and supplies 'only by mastering the sea'. Mark the gap, do not invent the missing words.
proposed_fix: and reflecting that only in this way could he prevent the crossing of the land army and in general ward the war off from Asia [text missing in the Greek] ... securely command the sea, he resolved to fight a naval battle

quote: During the season of that sacrifice, the law requires that these Salii not change their location for thirty days, wherever they may happen to be caught.
problem: The Greek has a lacuna (`*` / `**`) between 'τοῖς θεοῖς:' and 'τριακονθήμερον μὴ μεταβαίνειν κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς θυσίας, ἐν ᾗ ποτ᾽ ἂν χώρᾳ καταληφθῶσιν [οἱ σάλιοι οὗτοι]'. The sentence begins mid-clause; 'the law requires' is not in the Greek and 'these Salii' is an editorial bracket. The English reads as if whole.
proposed_fix: [Text lost] ... not to move for thirty days at the time of the sacrifice, in whatever place they may be caught [these Salii].

quote: the Romans took possession of Sardis and its citadel, and then Musaeus came from Antiochus under flag of truce.
problem: Greek: 'τὰς Σάρδεις καὶ τὰς ἀκροπόλεις ἄρτι *** ἧκε Μουσαῖος' - a lacuna stands after ἄρτι and the verb of the first clause is missing; English joins the two clauses seamlessly. Also ἀκροπόλεις is plural.
proposed_fix: the Romans took possession of Sardis and the citadels, just then [text lost] ... and Musaeus came from Antiochus to negotiate.

quote: Publius said that the Romans never became harsher after victory.
problem: Greek 'οὔτε νικήσαντας ἔφη Ῥωμαίους οὐδέποτε γενέσθαι βαρυτέρους, *' ends in a lacuna (continued by '** διὸ'); the οὔτε has no matching clause, so the sentence is incomplete and probably corrupt. English presents it as complete.
proposed_fix: Publius said that the Romans, when victorious, never became harsher [text lost] ...

quote: So they separated on those terms, and in the following days the Romans divided their forces.
problem: Greek 'ταῖς δ᾽ ἑξῆς ἡμέραις οἱ Ῥωμαῖοι διεῖλον τὰς δυνάμεις * ** μετὰ δέ τινας ἡμέρας παραγενομένων τῶν ὁμήρων' has a lacuna after διεῖλον τὰς δυνάμεις; English runs straight on to the arrival of the hostages.
proposed_fix: So they separated on those terms, and in the following days the Romans divided their forces [text lost] ...

quote: but would continue entirely to leave those matters in Roman hands.
problem: Greek 'ἀλλὰ μεῖναι *** τελέως διδοὺς ἐκείνοις τὴν ἐξουσίαν' has a lacuna after μεῖναι; the English supplies a smooth 'would continue ... to leave'.
proposed_fix: but ... [text lost] ... entirely giving them the authority.

quote: I would never knowingly give way to any living man.
problem: Greek 'οὐδέποτ᾽ ἂν οὐδενὶ τῶν ὄντων ἐκχωρήσαιμι κατὰ δύναμιν': κατὰ δύναμιν = 'so far as lies in my power', not 'knowingly'.
proposed_fix: I would never give way to anyone in the world, so far as lies in my power.

quote: being the first in Asia and Greece to share your friendship and alliance
problem: Greek 'πρῶτος μετασχὼν τῆς ὑμετέρας φιλίας καὶ συμμαχίας, σχεδὸν πάντων τῶν [κατὰ] τὴν Ἀσίαν καὶ τὴν Ἑλλάδα νεμομένων': σχεδὸν ('almost') is dropped; he was first of almost all those dwelling in Asia and Greece.
proposed_fix: being the first of almost all who live in Asia and Greece to share your friendship and alliance

quote: can be given by you to whomever you wish.
problem: Greek has a lacuna here: ἔξεστιν ὑμῖν οἷς ἂν βούλησθε * / ** προστεθέντα. The infinitive governing the list (Lycaonia, Hellespontine Phrygia, Pisidia, Chersonese) and the connection to προστεθέντα are lost; the English reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: can be given by you to whomever you wish [gap in the Greek text here].

quote: while those that had paid tribute to Antiochus alone should have that tribute remitted.
problem: Greek: ὅσαι δ᾽ Ἀντιόχῳ, μόνον ταύταις ἀφεῖσθαι τὸν φόρον. μόνον goes with ταύταις: only the cities that had paid Antiochus are released from tribute. English 'Antiochus alone' reads as cities that paid no one but Antiochus, which shifts the sense.
proposed_fix: while only those that had paid tribute to Antiochus should have that tribute remitted.

quote: the Scipios and Lucius
problem: Greek: οἵ τε περὶ τὸν Σκιπίωνα καὶ Λεύκιον — singular Σκιπίωνα, i.e. Scipio and his party (the earlier τοὺς περὶ τὸν Σκιπίωνα is rendered 'Scipio' in the same chapter), plus Lucius (apparently Aemilius Regillus, the naval victor). 'The Scipios' makes the name plural and changes who arrives.
proposed_fix: Scipio and his party, and Lucius

quote: and Philip’s weakness there
problem: Greek: τὰ περὶ τοὺς Ἀθαμᾶνας καὶ τὴν τοῦ Φιλίππου *** — there is a lacuna after τοῦ Φιλίππου. 'weakness there' is supplied, not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: and Philip’s [gap in the Greek text]

quote: These broke through the enemy entrenchment lying between and slipped into the city.
problem: Greek: εἰσέφρησαν εἰς τὴν πόλιν, * / ** παραγγείλας — the genitive absolute about Nicander has no main verb, and a lacuna follows. English reads on as if complete.
proposed_fix: These broke through the enemy entrenchment lying between and slipped into the city. [gap in the Greek text]

quote: He had instructed them that on the agreed day they were to sally out, while he himself would join in and support the danger.
problem: Greek: αὐτοὺς μὲν ἐξελθόντας *** ποιήσασθαι — a lacuna after ἐξελθόντας; the object of ποιήσασθαι is missing. The subject of παραγγείλας also stands after a lacuna.
proposed_fix: [Nicander] having instructed them that on the agreed day they were to sally out and [gap in the Greek text], while he himself would join them in the danger.

quote: They rushed boldly out of the city and fought gallantly
problem: Greek begins *** αὐτῶν μὲν εὐψύχως τῆς πόλεως ἐξορμησάντων — a lacuna precedes this clause; English begins as if continuous.
proposed_fix: [gap in the Greek text] When they rushed boldly out of the city and fought gallantly

quote: oak beams wrapped in tow
problem: Greek: στύπη δρύινα, 'oak logs/stumps'. 'Wrapped in tow' has no counterpart in the Greek.
proposed_fix: oak logs

quote: urging them to save themselves, and warning that destruction was not far off if they did not take better counsel for themselves.
problem: The Greek has a lacuna (***) after παρακαλῶν σῴζειν σφᾶς αὐτούς; the following clause εἶναι δὲ τοῦτον οὐ μακράν has no surviving antecedent for τοῦτον. The English smooths this by supplying 'destruction'.
proposed_fix: urging them to save themselves [gap in the Greek] and saying that this was not far off if they did not take better counsel for themselves.

quote: In particular Leon son of Hicesias seemed to have spoken well in other respects
problem: Greek: καὶ γὰρ ἐδόκει μετὰ Δάμων᾽ ὁ Κιχησίου λέων ἄλλα τε καλῶς εἰπεῖν. 'For' (καὶ γάρ, explaining why the senate relented) and the words μετὰ Δάμωνα (after Damon) are dropped; the patronymic Κιχησίου is Cichesias, not Hicesias.
proposed_fix: For Leon son of Cichesias, speaking after Damon, seemed to have spoken well in other respects

quote: The people of the Aetolians shall maintain the rule and supremacy of the Roman people in good faith.
problem: Greek: τὴν ἀρχὴν καὶ τὴν δυναστείαν τοῦ δήμου τῶν Ῥωμαίων * **. The sentence breaks off in a lacuna; the verb and 'in good faith' are not in the Greek, they are invented to smooth the gap.
proposed_fix: The people of the Aetolians shall ... the rule and supremacy of the Roman people [gap in the Greek].

quote: And whenever the Romans are at war with anyone, the people of the Aetolians shall also be at war with them.
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) immediately before καὶ ἐὰν πολεμῶσιν πρός τινας Ῥωμαῖοι; the English reads on as if the text were continuous and the clause were a plain continuation of the preceding clause.
proposed_fix: [gap in the Greek] ... and if the Romans are at war with anyone, the people of the Aetolians shall be at war with them.

quote: he took measures to prevent any importation of funds gathered from outside.
problem: Greek: περιεβα... γένοιτο κομιδὴ τῶν ἔξω ποριζομένων χρημάτων. The word περιεβα... is truncated/corrupt, but there is no negative (no μή); γένοιτο κομιδή means there should be a bringing-in of funds procured from abroad. The English inverts the sense ('prevent') and hides the break.
proposed_fix: he [the Greek breaks off here] ... so that there might be a supply of funds procured from outside.

quote: but that in his whole strength and conduct he deserved to be stripped of power and punished
problem: The Greek has a marked gap: ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τὴν ῥώμην ὅλην* εἰς καθαίρεσιν τῆς ἀρχῆς καὶ ἐπιστροφῆς εἶναι καὶ κολάσεως. The text breaks off after ὅλην; 'and conduct' is invented and the sentence is smoothed over as if whole.
proposed_fix: but that, in view of his whole power [text lost here], he was liable to removal from his rule, to correction, and to punishment

quote: dealt with each as policy required in their interviews
problem: Greek: τὴν προειρημένην δόξαν ἐνεργασάμενος ἑκάστοις κατὰ τὰς ἐντεύξεις, 'having produced in each of them, at the interviews, the impression already mentioned'. The English substitutes a different idea ('as policy required') and drops the reference back to the earlier-mentioned impression.
proposed_fix: created in each of them, in their interviews, the impression already described

quote: from the city named Sinda
problem: Greek: ἐκ τῆς Ἰσίνδης προσαγορευομένης πόλεως; the city is Isinda (people: Ἰσινδεῖς).
proposed_fix: from the city named Isinda

quote: relieved the people of Sinda from the siege
problem: Greek: τοὺς Ἰσινδεῖς ἐξελόμενος ἐκ τῆς πολιορκίας; the people of Isinda.
proposed_fix: relieved the people of Isinda from the siege

quote: In the affair concerning Ariarathes, the outcome became proverbial: though they had matters in hand, they came to grief at the hands of their enemies.
problem: The Greek is fragmentary: ἐν... η... τῆς πράξεως τῆς περὶ τὸν Ἀριαράθην εἰς τὴν παροιμίαν: ἔχοντες γὰρ π... διετε... οι τοῖς πολεμίοις ἐγένοντο. Words are lost at the start, and in ἔχοντες γὰρ π... διετε... οι; the English reads as a complete sentence and supplies 'outcome' and 'came to grief', which are not in the surviving text.
proposed_fix: [text lost] of the affair concerning Ariarathes [text lost] into the proverb; for having [text lost] they [text lost] fell to their enemies.

quote: He was to evacuate the cities and territory specified.
problem: The Greek reads ἐκχωρείτω δὲ πόλεων καὶ χώρας * **. - the text breaks off after χώρας (lacuna marked by asterisks); the list of cities and territory is lost. The English reads on as if the clause were whole and implies a specification that is not in the surviving text.
proposed_fix: He was to withdraw from cities and territory [...]. [The text is broken off here; the list of places is lost.]

quote: at the season when he also paid the Romans
problem: Greek τῷ ἐπιβαλλομένῳ * καιρῷ, ᾧ καὶ τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις ἀποδίδωσι has a single-asterisk gap after ἐπιβαλλομένῳ that the English does not mark; the verb is also present tense (ἀποδίδωσι).
proposed_fix: at the appropriate [...] time, at which he also pays the Romans

quote: and his brother Lucius
problem: Greek Λεύκιον τὸν ἀδελφόν has no genitive; the subject of the sentence is ὁ στρατηγός, so Lucius is the commander's brother (Lucius Manlius, brother of Gnaeus Manlius Vulso), not a brother of Thermus. English 'his brother' reads as Thermus's brother, which is a wrong identity.
proposed_fix: and Lucius, the commander's brother

quote: both the power and the protected standing of Sparta
problem: Greek: τὴν δύναμιν καὶ τὴν προστασίαν καταλελύσθαι τὴν Λακεδαιμονίων. προστασία here is leadership/headship (primacy), not 'protection' or 'protected standing'.
proposed_fix: both the power and the leadership of the Spartans

quote: which had previously been entered against them, to be publicly proclaimed.
problem: Greek breaks off here: ἃς ἦσαν πρότερον αὐτοῖς ἐπιγεγραμμένοι, * (lacuna). English runs on as if the sentence were whole.
proposed_fix: which had previously been entered against them, to be publicly proclaimed [gap in the Greek]

quote: Thus in one case they condemned them for sacrilege
problem: Greek resumes after a second lacuna: ** καὶ τούτῳ τῷ τρόπῳ τῶν δικῶν μίαν μὲν αὐτῶν κατεδίκασαν ἱεροσυλίας. Gap not marked; 'Thus' smooths over it.
proposed_fix: [gap in the Greek] ... and in this way, of the suits, in one case they condemned them for sacrilege

quote: For when there was a clash over the seizure of the herds of Myrrichus and Simon
problem: Greek: παραυτίκα γὰρ ἔλαχε * ** τῶν Μυρρίχου θρεμμάτων καὶ τοῦ Σίμωνος. There is a lacuna after ἔλαχε ('obtained by lot / fell to'); 'seizure' is invented and the gap is smoothed.
proposed_fix: For at once [subject lost] obtained by lot [gap in the Greek] of the herds of Myrrichus and Simon; and when a clash arose over this

quote: after envoys intervened and settlements were arranged
problem: Greek: διαπρεσβευσαμένων *** τοῖς συναλλάγμασιν. A lacuna follows διαπρεσβευσαμένων (negotiating by embassy) and the construction with τοῖς συναλλάγμασιν is lost; English supplies a complete clause.
proposed_fix: after negotiating by embassy [gap in the Greek] the agreements

quote: and sternly rebuked the Lycians, they declared that they would endure anything rather than do what the Rhodians ordered.
problem: Greek: προσεπετίμησε τοῖς Λυκίοις *** πᾶν γὰρ ὑπομένειν ἔφασαν μᾶλλον ἢ ... A lacuna follows τοῖς Λυκίοις; the ὡς δέ clause has no main verb, and the Lycian reply is introduced by γάρ ('for'). English joins them into one smooth sentence.
proposed_fix: and sternly rebuked the Lycians [gap in the Greek]; for they said that they would endure anything rather than do what the Rhodians ordered.

quote: disapproved of both the treatment of the walls and the killings at Compasium
problem: Greek: τῇ τῶν τειχῶν συντελέσει* καὶ τῇ καταλύσει *** τῶν ἐν τῷ Κομπασίῳ διαφθαρέντων. There is a lacuna after συντελέσει and another after καταλύσει, both unmarked in English; 'killings' replaces a gapped phrase (καταλύσις ... τῶν διαφθαρέντων, 'the putting down/ending ... of those destroyed').
proposed_fix: disapproved of both the completion of the walls [gap in the Greek] and the putting down [gap in the Greek] of those who perished at Compasium

quote: it advised the envoys whom the Achaeans regularly sent from time to time to pay close attention and to show the reception that was fitting
problem: Greek: τοῖς δὲ πρεσβευταῖς τοῖς αἰεὶ παρ᾽ ἑαυτῶν ἐκπεμπομένοις παρῄνει προσέχειν τὸν νοῦν καὶ καταδοχὴν ποιεῖσθαι τὴν ἁρμόζουσαν. The subject is the senate; παρ᾽ ἑαυτῶν means 'from the senate's own side', so the envoys are the ones Rome sends out. The dative recipients (τοῖς ... πρεσβευταῖς, with the infinitives) are the Achaeans being advised to pay attention and give a fitting reception to Roman envoys, just as the Romans receive envoys who come to them (καθάπερ καὶ Ῥωμαῖοι ποιοῦνται τῶν παραγινομένων πρὸς αὐτοὺς πρεσβευτῶν). The current English makes them Achaean envoys, which inverts the sense. Note: strictly the dative τοῖς πρεσβευταῖς is the object of προσέχειν (pay attention to the envoys), with Achaeans as understood addressees.
proposed_fix: it advised the Achaeans to pay close attention to the envoys whom it sent out from time to time and to give them the reception that was fitting

quote: the man who had actually carried out the deed, so that the senate, as they said, might learn the facts from him
problem: Greek: τὸν αὐθέντην γεγονότα τῆς πράξεως, ὡς ἐκεῖνοί φασιν, ἵνα πύθηται παρὰ τούτου τὰς ἀληθείας ἡ σύγκλητος. 'ὡς ἐκεῖνοί φασιν' (as they [Appius and colleagues] say) qualifies the claim that Cassander was the author of the deed, not the purpose clause. English attaches 'as they said' to the senate's learning the facts.
proposed_fix: the man who, as they said, had been the author of the deed, so that the senate might learn the truth from him

quote: Calling him king and offspring of gods, they said that if he abused such a name he might perhaps obtain some pity and pardon for what had happened
problem: Greek is a badly damaged papyrus text: βασιλέα καὶ θ̣ε̣ω̣ν̣ α̣ι̣μ̣α̣ τοῦτον λέγοντες καταχρώμενοι τ̣ε̣υ̣ξ̣ε̣σ̣θ̣α̣ι̣ τινος ἐλέους καὶ συγγνώμης ἐπὶ τῳ... σασθαι τ̣ο̣ν̣ β̣α̣σ̣ι̣λεα... Only 'calling this man king and blood (αἷμα) of gods', '[to] obtain some pity and pardon' and 'the king' survive. The conditional 'if he abused such a name', 'perhaps' and 'for what had happened' are not in the Greek; the lacunae are silently smoothed into a complete sentence.
proposed_fix: Calling him king and 'blood of gods' [text lost] ... [that he would] obtain some pity and pardon [text lost] ... the king ...

quote: yet it would have been more kingly not to be the first to break faith, but rather to let others violate agreements before he did so himself
problem: Greek: ων γε μὴν καὶ βασιλικώτερος.... ονων ων ἀθετηθῆναι γὰρ υ̣φ̣ ε̣τ̣ε̣ρων κ̣ρ̣ε̣ι̣τ̣τ̣ον ἦν ἢ πρότερον αὐτὸν ἀθετεῖν τὰς πίστεις καὶ μὴν ἀδικεῖσθαι μᾶλλον η... Only 'more kingly' (βασιλικώτερος) survives before a gap; the surviving clause is 'for it was better to be betrayed by others than himself first to break his pledges', followed by 'and indeed to be wronged rather than ...' (broken off). English invents 'yet it would have been more kingly' as a whole judgment and omits the following 'to be wronged rather than' clause.
proposed_fix: ... and more kingly still [text lost] ... for it was better to be betrayed by others than to be the first himself to break his pledges; and indeed to be wronged rather than [text lost] ...

quote: They said that all men admire Philip for his greatness of spirit
problem: Greek: ... ς θαυμάζουσι μὲν πάντες Φίλιππον διὰ τὴν ορ [gap] ... ς μεγαλοψυχίαν. 'They said' is not in the Greek (it is in the damaged lead-in only), and there are gaps both before θαυμάζουσι and between 'διὰ τὴν ορ' and 'μεγαλοψυχίαν' (a lost qualifier of the greatness of spirit); the English reads on as whole.
proposed_fix: [text lost] ... all men admire Philip for his [text lost] ... greatness of spirit

quote: Ptolemy, by contrast, bound the men naked to carts
problem: Greek: *** πλὴν ὅγε Πτολεμαῖος δήσας τοὺς ἀνθρώπους γυμνοὺς ταῖς ἁμάξαις εἷλκε. The sentence is preceded by a marked lacuna (***); πλὴν ὅγε means 'except that Ptolemy, for his part', and the identity of the 'men' is lost with the gap. English smooths the gap into a continuous contrast.
proposed_fix: [text lost] ... except that Ptolemy for his part bound the men naked to carts

quote: she preserved toward all of them without surpassing measure the same goodwill and motherly affection down to the end of her life
problem: Greek: πρὸς πάντας τούτους ἀνυπέρβλητον διεφύλαξε τὴν εὔνοιαν καὶ φιλοστοργίαν. ἀνυπέρβλητον means 'unsurpassable/unsurpassed'; 'without surpassing measure' reads as 'without excess' (inverts the sense), and 'the same' has no Greek counterpart.
proposed_fix: she preserved toward all of them unsurpassed goodwill and motherly affection down to the end of her life

quote: Ostiagon the Galatian, king of the Galatians in Asia
problem: Greek: Ὀρτιάγων ὁ Γαλάτης. The name is Ortiagon (so also in Book 21, 'Chiomara, the wife of Ortiagon'); 'Ostiagon' is a misrendering and breaks identity with the Book 21 figure. The chapter heading carries the same form.
proposed_fix: Ortiagon the Galatian, king of the Galatians in Asia

quote: and they all addressed arguments against the Achaeans suited to their own particular causes
problem: The Greek has a lacuna (`* ** ἐποιοῦντο πρὸς τοὺς Ἀχαιοὺς οἰκείους ταῖς ἰδίαις ὑποθέσεσι λόγους`); the subject of ἐποιοῦντο is lost in the gap. English supplies 'and they all' and renders πρὸς τοὺς Ἀχαιοὺς as 'against', neither of which the surviving Greek gives (πρός + acc. = 'to/with regard to').
proposed_fix: made speeches to the Achaeans suited to their own particular causes

quote: learned that he was displaying habits and tastes ill suited to the situation
problem: Greek: μαθεῖν ὡς ἀνοίκειον ὑπόθεσιν τῆς ἰδίας αἱρέσεως καὶ φύσεως ἀποδέδωκε, 'that he had put forward an undertaking alien to his own choice and nature'. ἀνοίκειον takes the genitive of his own character; it is not 'unsuited to the situation'.
proposed_fix: learned that he had set before himself an undertaking ill suited to his own inclination and nature

quote: also took action against their sons
problem: epaneilen (epanaireo) means 'killed in addition'; Greek says Philip killed the sons as well, not merely 'took action against' them.
proposed_fix: also killed their sons

quote: for so long because, obeying the ephors as though they were parents, they endured
problem: tosouton chronon ... hoson (correlative): they preserved the hegemony for just as long as they obeyed the ephors and endured joint kingship; English turns the temporal correlative into a causal 'because'.
proposed_fix: for just as long as, obeying the ephors as though they were parents, they endured

quote: carry their anger against their own people so far
problem: homophylous means those of the same race/kindred (i.e. fellow Greeks), not 'their own people'; as written the English contradicts the immediate object 'their enemies'.
proposed_fix: carry their anger against men of their own race so far

quote: by the war. * The Messenians had long
problem: Greek has a gap (* / ** before palai men hoi Messenioi) and the sentence resumes mid-thought; English marks it only with a bare asterisk and reads on as if whole, unlike the [...] used for the other lacunae in the chapter.
proposed_fix: by the war. [...] The Messenians had long

quote: both because the gift seemed worthy of gratitude and because the expense appeared to amount to not much less than ten talents
problem: The Greek sentence about cost is a separate bracketed gloss, [δοκεῖ γὰρ ἡ δαπάνη οὐ πολὺ λείπειν τῶν δέκα ταλάντων], 'for the cost seems to fall little short of ten talents'. It is not a second reason given by the Achaeans, and the editorial brackets (a suspected interpolation) are silently dropped.
proposed_fix: because the gift seemed worthy of gratitude. [For the cost seems to fall little short of ten talents.]

quote: on the pretext of keeping their own laws and decrees in force
problem: Greek has χάριν τοῦ διαμένειν τοὺς νόμους ἰσχυροὺς καὶ τὰ δόγματα, 'for the sake of keeping the laws and decrees strong'. It states their purpose; there is no word for 'pretext'.
proposed_fix: for the sake of keeping their own laws and decrees in force

quote: And since the Achaean nation had grown and advanced in the best direction from the period covered by my history, this in turn became the beginning of its change for the worse: the audacity of Callicrates.
problem: οὕτω δὲ τοῦ τῶν Ἀχαιῶν ἔθνους ηὐξημένου … αὕτη πάλιν ἀρχὴ … ἐγένετο μεταβολῆς is 'Thus, with the nation having grown … this again became the beginning of the change'. It is not causal 'since'. The Greek then breaks off after τὸ Καλλικράτους θράσος * with a marked lacuna, which the English smooths over.
proposed_fix: Thus, with the Achaean nation having grown and advanced in the best direction from the period covered by my history, this in turn became the beginning of its change for the worse: the audacity of Callicrates [text lost here].

quote: The Romans, being human beings
problem: The Greek has a second lacuna (** Ῥωμαῖοι ὄντες ἄνθρωποι …) before this sentence. The passage begins mid-thought and is not a continuation of the Callicrates sentence, but the English reads on as if whole.
proposed_fix: […] The Romans, being human beings

quote: But whenever someone reminds them of what is just, having kept faith, they draw back
problem: τετηρηκὼς τὴν πίστιν is nominative singular and agrees with τις ('someone who has kept faith'), not with the Romans. The English attaches it to the Romans.
proposed_fix: But whenever someone who has kept faith reminds them of what is just, they draw back

quote: to add to the other evils, he did so by bribery
problem: πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις κακοῖς καὶ δωροδοκηθείς is passive, 'was bribed (took bribes)'. It does not say he won the office by bribing others, so the English reverses who paid whom.
proposed_fix: besides his other misdeeds, he was himself bribed

quote: Instead he said they must first make a legal case, and then press their claim again; and if even then they failed to persuade, one should at last yield under protest
problem: Subject is the Achaeans: ἔφη δεῖν δικαιολογεῖσθαι, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα πάλιν ἀξιοῦν, εἰ δὲ μηδ᾽ οὕτως πείθοιεν (the Romans). The English 'they' reads as the Romans making the case and failing to persuade, which makes no sense with 'one should yield'.
proposed_fix: Instead he said that one must first plead one's case, and then make the request again; and if even so one failed to persuade the Romans, one should at last yield, calling witnesses to one's protest

quote: one must be of one mind with the Romans in present circumstances
problem: The Greek here is a fragment after a gap: 'εἰ δὲ μηδ᾽ ὁ Φιλοποίμην εἰπεῖν τοῦτο τολμᾷ... καιροῖς ἕνα Ῥωμαίοις' (text lost before καιροῖς, and again after). There is no verb or clause for 'one must be of one mind'; the English invents a connected clause and smooths the lacuna.
proposed_fix: [...] occasions [...] one [...] the Romans [...]

quote: unwillingly and with hesitation
problem: 'ἀκουσίως δὲ τοῦτο πράττοντας καὶ μετὰ προσκοπῆς': προσκοπή is offence/resentment, not hesitation.
proposed_fix: unwillingly and with resentment

quote: for as long as we can
problem: 'ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον, ἐφ᾽ ὅσον μέλλομεν τελέως...' breaks off after τελέως (lacuna). The English closes the sentence as if whole and renders it with a different sense.
proposed_fix: for as long as we are going to completely [...]

quote: And even if they do issue commands, by reminding them
problem: Greek has a gap before and after: '... κἂν ἐπιτάττωσιν... καὶ τούτων ὑπομιμνήσκοντες'. The protasis is incomplete and the English joins it smoothly.
proposed_fix: [...] even if they issue commands [...] and by reminding them

quote: and after six more days’ march they moved on to Parnassus
problem: 'ἑκταῖοι πάλιν ἀνέζευξαν εἰς Παρνασσόν' parallels πεμπταῖοι: 'on the sixth day they marched on again to Parnassus'. Greek gives an ordinal day, not 'six more days' march' (a different number and sense).
proposed_fix: and on the sixth day they marched on again to Parnassus

quote: the armies broke up and marched away from the place
problem: ὧν καὶ παραγενηθέντων ἐξ αὐτῆς ἀνέζευξαν αἱ δυνάμεις: ἐξ αὐτῆς is the adverbial idiom 'immediately, at once' (sc. ὥρας), not 'from the place'; ἀνέζευξαν = broke camp.
proposed_fix: the armies at once broke camp and withdrew

quote: each of the upper-deck rowers
problem: τῶν ἀφρακτιτῶν: from ἄφρακτος, an open or undecked ship, so the men of the undecked ships. Upper-deck rowers would be θρανῖται, which is not what the Greek says.
proposed_fix: each of the crews of the undecked ships

quote: when it still did not seem likely that the Lycians would once again revolt
problem: ὅσον οὔπω δοκούντων πάλιν ἐπαναστήσεσθαι τῶν Λυκίων: ὅσον οὔπω means 'all but now, on the point of', so the Lycians seemed about to rise again. The English reverses this and says a revolt seemed unlikely.
proposed_fix: when the Lycians seemed on the point of rising again

quote: with only two or three companions
problem: Greek ἀλύων ἐφαίνετο δεύτερος καὶ τρίτος: he appeared as 'second and third', i.e. himself plus one or two others (one or two companions), not two or three companions.
proposed_fix: with only one or two companions

quote: were making a tour of the islands and the cities in Asia and spent the greatest part of their time in Rhodes, though in those days the Rhodians had no need of supervision
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) after τὰς κατὰ τὴν Ἀσίαν πόλεις, before πλεῖστον δ᾽ ἐν τῇ Ῥόδῳ; the English reads on as if whole. Also οὐ προσδεομένων τῶν Ῥωμαίων has no stated object ('supervision' is invented); the missing object presumably stood in the gap.
proposed_fix: were making a tour of the islands and the cities in Asia [gap in the Greek] ... and most of all in Rhodes, although the Rhodians at that time did not need it

quote: After the conference with the Romans and the Greek states, Perseus set down
problem: Greek: μετὰ τὸν σύλλογον τὸν πρὸς τοὺς Ῥωμαίους, *** τῶν Ἑλλήνων, a lacuna after 'Romans' before τῶν Ἑλλήνων; the 'conference with ... the Greek states' is invented smoothing.
proposed_fix: After the conference with the Romans, [gap in the Greek] ... of the Greeks, Perseus set down

quote: Antenor and his colleagues did not accept that answer; but, satisfied with the rest
problem: Greek: τὴν μὲν ἀπόκρισιν οὐκ ἔλαβον ***, τὴν δὲ λοιπὴν φιλανθρωπίαν ἀποδεξάμενοι: lacuna after οὐκ ἔλαβον; the verb is 'did not receive/take' with something lost, and 'did not accept' resolves it silently.
proposed_fix: Antenor and his colleagues did not receive the answer [gap in the Greek] ...; but, satisfied with the rest

quote: ordered them to leave Rome at once, and all other Macedonians who happened to be staying in Italy to depart within thirty days
problem: Greek: προσέταξαν αὐτοῖς ἐκ μὲν τῆς Ῥώμης εὐθέως ἀπαλλάττεσθαι καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασιν Μακεδόσιν ... ἐκ δὲ τῆς Ἰταλίας ἐν τριάκονθ᾽ ἡμέραις ἐκχωρεῖν: the envoys AND the other Macedonians must leave Rome at once, and (all) leave Italy within thirty days. English attaches 'thirty days' only to the other Macedonians and drops the two-stage order.
proposed_fix: ordered them and all the other Macedonians who happened to be staying there to leave Rome at once, and to leave Italy within thirty days

quote: the remaining one to Tenedos under a commander named Timagoras
problem: Greek: τὴν δὲ μίαν εἰς Τένεδον, ἐφ᾽ ἧς ἄρχων ἐπέπλει * Τιμαγόρας. There is a gap (*) before Τιμαγόρας; the text is damaged and the commander of the Tenedos ship is not securely named. English supplies 'a commander named Timagoras', duplicating the commander of the five ships, as if whole.
proposed_fix: the remaining one to Tenedos, on which a commander sailed [gap in the Greek] ... Timagoras

quote: whether they knew that he was fighting unfairly
problem: Greek: πότερον οὐ συνοίδασιν αὐτῷ ποιοῦντι τὰ δίκαια κατὰ τὴν ἄθλησιν - 'do they not realize that he (Cleitomachus, in indirect speech) is acting justly/fairly in the contest'. The English drops the οὐ and inverts the sense to 'unfairly'.
proposed_fix: whether they were not aware that he himself was fighting fairly

quote: in defiance of every principle of justice.
problem: Greek ends πρότερος *** - the text breaks off after 'first' (lacuna); the English closes the sentence as if complete.
proposed_fix: in defiance of every principle of justice [the text breaks off here].

quote: had been the first to lay hands on territory that was not his
problem: Greek: Πτολεμαῖος αὐτῷ παρὰ πάντα τὰ δίκαια τὰς χεῖρας ἐπιβάλλει πρότερος. The dative αὐτῷ is Antiochus: Ptolemy lays hands on HIM (Antiochus) first, against all justice. 'Territory that was not his' is not in the Greek and turns the charge into one about land, reversing who is the wronged party in the claim.
proposed_fix: had been the first to lay hands on him

quote: saying that he would somehow make Gentius well disposed
problem: Greek has a lacuna: φάσκων ἐξιγμένον *** εὐνοοῦντα ποιήσειν τὸν Γένθιον. English smooths it with an invented 'somehow'.
proposed_fix: saying that [...] he would make Gentius well disposed

quote: would have been won over
problem: πάντας ἂν συνέβη ... τοὺς πλείστους ἐξελεγχθῆναι: ἐξελέγχω means to be tested/exposed/shown up, not 'won over'. Greek does not say they would be won over.
proposed_fix: would have been put to the proof

quote: by good fortune he did not take that path
problem: νῦν δὲ καλῶς ποιῶν οὐκ ἦλθε ταύτην τὴν ὁδόν: 'doing well / acting rightly', not 'by good fortune' (no τύχη here).
proposed_fix: he did well not to take that path

quote: only a very few Greeks were driven into utter folly at the crisis of the action
problem: δι᾽ ἧς ὀλίγοι τελέως ἠλογήθησαν τῶν Ἑλλήνων ὑπὸ τὸν τῆς πράξεως καιρόν: ἀλογέω = to disregard/neglect; 'few were utterly disregarded'. No 'folly'.
proposed_fix: by which few of the Greeks were utterly disregarded at the time of the action

quote: King Ptolemy had applied to the Achaeans because the customary rites performed for kings when they come of age had now taken place in his case
problem: περὶ τοῦ βασιλέως Πτολεμαίου προσπεσόντος τοῖς Ἀχαιοῖς διότι γέγονεν αὐτῷ τὰ νομιζόμενα...ἀνακλητήρια: προσπίπτω = news reached; the Achaeans received word, Ptolemy did not apply to them. διότι is 'that', not 'because'.
proposed_fix: word reached the Achaeans concerning King Ptolemy that the customary ceremonies (the anaklētēria) performed for kings when they come of age had now taken place in his case

quote: his fellow envoys were to send word back at once explaining this
problem: τοὺς μὲν συμπρεσβευτὰς ἐξ αὐτῆς πέμπειν διασαφήσοντας: Polybius is to send his colleagues off at once to report; the colleagues are the object, not the subject.
proposed_fix: he was to send his fellow envoys off at once to report this

quote: decide the whole issue by force of arms
problem: λήψεσθαι τὰ ὅλα κρίσιν ἐκ τῶν κατὰ λόγον: 'the whole matter would be decided, as was to be expected / in the natural course'; no mention of arms. Phrase possibly corrupt.
proposed_fix: decide the whole issue, as was to be expected

quote: Alcithon and Pasiadas
problem: Ἀλκίθον is accusative of Ἀλκίθος (cf. Ch. 19 Ἀλκίθος); name should be Alcithus.
proposed_fix: Alcithus and Pasiadas

quote: Agesilochus son of Hegesias was sent to Rome, along with Nicagoras son of Nicander
problem: Ἁγησίλοχος Ἁγησίου, Νικαγόρας, Νίκανδρος: three separate envoys (Nicander is a man, not Nicagoras' father); English drops one envoy.
proposed_fix: Agesilochus son of Hegesias, Nicagoras and Nicander were sent to Rome

quote: the envoys sent to arrange a settlement joined the envoys from Greece
problem: Greek: συνῆψαν τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἑλλάδος πρεσβευτῶν οἱ πεμφθέντες ἐπὶ τὰς διαλύσεις. The genitive is partitive: 'those of the envoys from Greece who had been sent to arrange a settlement' are the subject (verb συνάπτω, 'met/came up'). English invents two separate groups of envoys; the following speakers (Achaeans, Athenians, Eudemus of Miletus) are all the Greek envoys.
proposed_fix: those of the envoys from Greece who had been sent to arrange a settlement came to meet him

quote: to the king’s youth
problem: Greek: τὴν συγγένειαν καὶ τὴν ἡλικίαν τὴν τοῦ Πτολεμαίου. Both kinship and youth belong to Ptolemy; 'the king' after 'Antiochus' reads as Antiochus.
proposed_fix: to Ptolemy’s youth

quote: appointed Parmenion and Marcus
problem: Greek has Μόρκον (Morcus, an Illyrian name), not the Roman Μᾶρκος; ch. 11 of the same book correctly reads Morcus.
proposed_fix: appointed Parmenion and Morcus

quote: That embassy also succeeded in persuading the Rhodians to join the war.
problem: Greek ἔπεισε δὲ καὶ τοὺς Ῥοδίους συνεμβαίνειν εἰς τὸν πόλεμον has no 'embassy' as subject; the subject is Perseus, continuing from the preceding sentence. The aorist is also odd against the Rhodians' actual course (ch. 10-11, they sue for peace), so the text may be corrupt or conative.
proposed_fix: He also persuaded the Rhodians to join in the war.

quote: and then, when he came close to the wall at Demetrias, spoke first with Menecrates and then with Antimachus
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) after τῷ τείχει, before ἐκοινολογεῖτο, and another (* ** ) after Ἀντιμάχῳ before εἴρηται; English reads on as if whole. Also τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ... τὸ δὲ δεύτερον = 'the first time ... the second time'.
proposed_fix: and again, when he came close to the wall at Demetrias, [text lost] he conversed, the first time with Menecrates and the second with Antimachus, [text lost]

quote: And the fact that Herophon twice went as an envoy from Perseus to Eumenes
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) between Ἡροφῶν and ἐπρέσβευσε that the English smooths over.
proposed_fix: And, further, that Herophon [text lost] twice went as envoy from Perseus to Eumenes

quote: Accordingly, Perseus’ dealings with the Gauls and with Gentius were of a piece with this—
problem: Greek ἀκολούθως δὲ τούτοις Περσεὺς καὶ τὰ πρὸς Γαλάτας καὶ τὰ πρὸς Γένθιον *** breaks off in a lacuna; the predicate is lost. English invents 'were of a piece with this' as if the sentence were complete.
proposed_fix: Accordingly, in keeping with this, Perseus’ affairs with the Gauls and with Gentius [text lost]

quote: as I have explained in my discussion of public speaking
problem: Greek has the bracketed [ὡς ἐν τῷ περὶ δημηγορίας τέθειται], passive 'as is set down in the (work) on public speaking', an editorial or cross-reference gloss in brackets, not a first-person statement by Polybius.
proposed_fix: [as is set down in the work on public speaking]

quote: When the envoys from Gentius, together with those led by Parmenio and Morcus and accompanied by Metrodorus, arrived at Rhodes
problem: Greek τῶν περὶ τὸν Παρμενίωνα καὶ Μόρκον, τῶν παρὰ τοῦ Γενθίου, καὶ σὺν τούτοις τοῦ Μητροδώρου: Parmenion and Morcus ARE the envoys from Gentius, and Metrodorus came with them. English wrongly implies two separate groups of envoys.
proposed_fix: When Parmenion and Morcus, the envoys from Gentius, and with them Metrodorus, arrived at Rhodes

quote: the number of cavalry that had been lost, and Gentius’ defection crushed them
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) before ἡ τοῦ Γενθίου μετάθεσις; English reads on as if whole.
proposed_fix: the number of cavalry that had been lost, and [text lost] Gentius’ change of side crushed them

quote: no one could say their treatment is adequate, so far as they develop them at all, because they have no material to work with
problem: οὐκ ἂν εἴποι τις ἀξίως ἐφ᾽ ὅσον ἐξεργάζονται διὰ τὴν ἀπορίαν τῶν πραγμάτων: no one could adequately say how far they elaborate (work up) these topics, owing to their poverty of real material. The English turns 'worthily describe the extent' into a judgment that their treatment is inadequate and 'if at all'.
proposed_fix: no one could adequately describe how far they work these up, given their lack of real material

quote: even if I should seem inconsistent in my subject matter, in my handling of events, or in my style of expression
problem: φανείημεν ἢ λήμμασι χρώμενοι τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἢ χειρισμῷ πραγμάτων ἢ τοῖς τῆς λέξεως ῥήμασι: if we appear to use the SAME themes, the same treatment of events, or the same turns of phrase (i.e. repetitiveness), not 'inconsistent'. Also the Greek has damaged text (οἷον εἰ τ̣...) just before.
proposed_fix: for instance if I should appear to be using the same themes, or the same treatment of events, or the same turns of phrase

quote: if I should sometimes slip in the names of mountains, rivers, or local places
problem: ἐάν που παραπίπτωμεν ἐν ὀνομασίαις ὀρῶν ἢ ποταμῶν ἢ τόπων ἰδιότησι: if we anywhere make slips (fall into error) in the names of mountains or rivers or the particular features of places; 'slip in' reads as 'insert'.
proposed_fix: if I should anywhere make slips in the names of mountains or rivers or in the particular features of places

quote: the siege of Phanoteia or Coroneia or Haliartus
problem: Greek has Φανοτείας καὶ Κορωνείας καὶ... ε... οῦ πολιορκίαν: the third name is lost in a lacuna (only fragments of letters); 'Haliartus' is invented and the list is 'and', not 'or'.
proposed_fix: the siege of Phanoteia and Coroneia and [name lost in a gap in the text]

quote: and beyond that to dwell on the capture of Tarentum, Corinth, Sardis, Gaza, Bactra, and, above all, Carthage
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) after πρὸς δὲ τούτοις before Τάραντος κατάληψιν; 'Corinth' is followed by a bracketed editorial supplement [πολιορκίαν]. The English reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: and beyond that [text missing] the capture of Tarentum, the [siege] of Corinth, Sardis, Gaza, Bactra, and above all the siege of Carthage

quote: Again, other writers have gone on at length about the Syrian war.
problem: Greek begins with a lacuna (***) then πάλιν ἕτεροι περὶ τοῦ Συριακοῦ πολέμου with no verb; 'have gone on at length' is supplied, not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: [text missing] Again, others on the Syrian war.

quote: what I have already explained more than once
problem: ὅπερ ἡμῖν εἴρηται διὰ πλειόνων: what has been said by us at greater length (at some length), not 'more than once'.
proposed_fix: what I have already explained at some length

quote: the rumor spread among many of Perseus’ Macedonians that it meant the king himself was being eclipsed
problem: ἐπὶ Περσέως τοῦ Μακεδόνος ἐκράτησεν ἡ φήμη παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς ὅτι βασιλέως ἔκλειψιν σημαίνει: Μακεδόνος is singular, 'Perseus the Macedonian' (in the time of Perseus), and the belief prevailed among most people generally, not just his Macedonians; it signifies the eclipse of a king (general).
proposed_fix: the belief prevailed among most people, in the time of Perseus the Macedonian, that it signified the eclipse of a king

quote: like anyone else
problem: εἰ καί τις ἄλλος: 'as much as anyone', i.e. he was as experienced in battles as anyone could be; 'like anyone else' makes him ordinary and drains the concession of καίτοι γε.
proposed_fix: as much as anyone

quote: pretending that he was sacrificing to Heracles—fitting cowardly rites for a cowardly man, and prayers that the god would not accept
problem: σκηψάμενος Ἡρακλεῖ θύειν, δειλὰ παρὰ δειλῶν ἱερὰ μὴ δεχομένῳ μηδ᾽ εὐχὰς ἀθεμίτους ἐπιτελοῦντι: the participles agree with Ἡρακλεῖ: Heracles does NOT accept cowardly sacrifices from cowards nor fulfil unlawful prayers. The English makes the rites 'fitting' and loses the negation on the god.
proposed_fix: pretending that he was sacrificing to Heracles, a god who does not accept cowardly offerings from cowards nor fulfil unlawful prayers

quote: while encamped in Thessaly for almost two years.
problem: Greek breaks off here: σχεδὸν ἐπὶ δύ᾽ ἐνιαυτοὺς * ** with a lacuna before τὸ δὲ παρέντας; the English closes the sentence as if complete.
proposed_fix: while encamped in Thessaly for almost two years [text missing here].

quote: When the party led by Hegesipolis entered
problem: Greek name is Ἁγέπολις (Hagepolis), not Hegesipolis.
proposed_fix: When the party of Hagepolis entered

quote: what the men around Hegesipolis said
problem: Ἁγέπολις (Hagepolis), as above.
proposed_fix: what the men around Hagepolis said

quote: For only in that way could a person show moderation even amid prosperity.
problem: καὶ γὰρ οὕτω μόλις ἂν ἐν ταῖς εὐκαιρίαις ἄνθρωπον μέτριον ὄντα φανῆναι: even so (i.e. even with this mindfulness) a man would scarcely/hardly appear moderate in times of success; the English turns 'hardly even so' into 'only in that way'.
proposed_fix: For even so, a man can hardly show himself moderate in times of prosperity.

quote: because she has used these blessings with them too
problem: διότι καὶ τούτοις ταῦτα τἀγαθὰ κέχρηκεν: κέχρηκεν is from χράω 'lend', Fortune has LENT these goods to them too, until she decides otherwise about them.
proposed_fix: because she has lent these blessings to them too

quote: whose name was scarcely known before
problem: ὧν οὐδ᾽ ὄνομα πρότερον ἦν γνώριμον: whose very name was not (even) known before; 'scarcely' weakens the negation.
proposed_fix: whose very name was not previously known

quote: with Lycortas to command the infantry and Polybius the cavalry
problem: ἡγεμόνα δὲ τῆς ὅλης συμμαχίας Λυκόρταν, τῶν δ᾽ ἱππέων Πολύβιον: Lycortas as commander of the whole allied force, not of the infantry only.
proposed_fix: with Lycortas as commander of the whole allied force and Polybius of the cavalry

quote: since Quintus Philippus was wintering in Macedonia.
problem: The Greek breaks off mid-phrase: τὴν παραχειμασίαν ἐν τῇ (text ends; the place is not given). 'Macedonia' is supplied and the sentence closed.
proposed_fix: since Quintus Philippus was wintering in the [text breaks off here]

quote: although the present king’s generosity was well known among them
problem: Greek has καὶ γὰρ ἡ τοῦ τότε βασιλεύοντος μεγαλοψυχία διάδηλος ἐγένετο τοῖς Ἕλλησιν: a γάρ clause (for indeed), not a concessive; it explains the limiting phrase 'in earlier times'. The 'although' reverses the logical link. The Greek here is somewhat compressed and the exact force of the γάρ is debatable.
proposed_fix: for the generosity of the king then reigning had been plain to the Greeks

quote: resumed the war against Ptolemy
problem: Greek ἐξήρτυε πόλεμον κατὰ Πτολεμαίου (imperfect of ἐξαρτύω, equip/prepare): Antiochus was preparing war, not yet resuming fighting.
proposed_fix: was preparing war against Ptolemy

quote: that the outcome in Alexandria and in the whole of Egypt was decided by it: that is, by the earlier decision of what should be done with Perseus
problem: Greek: τὰ κατὰ τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρειαν καὶ τὴν ὅλην Αἴγυπτον, καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἔσχατον καιρὸν ἐλθόντα, παρὰ τοῦτο πάλιν ὀρθωθῆναι, παρὰ τὸ φθάσαι κριθέντα τὰ κατὰ τὸν Περσέα πράγματα. Alexandria and Egypt, having come to the last extremity, were set upright again because the affair of Perseus had already been decided (the war ended). English omits the 'last extremity' and 'set upright again' and turns 'had been decided' into 'what should be done with Perseus'.
proposed_fix: that Alexandria and the whole of Egypt, though brought to the last extremity, were set upright again, simply because the affairs of Perseus had already been decided

quote: the answer that Agesipolis and his colleagues had obtained
problem: Greek has οἱ περὶ τὸν Ἁγέπολιν: the Rhodian envoy Hagepolis, not Agesipolis (a different name, Spartan).
proposed_fix: the answer that Hagepolis and his colleagues had obtained

quote: but that by giving special weight and dignity to the move they hoped to strip away the suspicions
problem: Greek: ἀλλὰ βουλόμενοι κατὰ τὴν ὑπέρθεσιν τῆς ἐπιβολῆς ἀφαιρεῖσθαι τὰς ὑπονοίας. ὑπέρθεσις means putting off, postponement, delay; nothing in it says 'special weight and dignity'. Sense: by the deferral of their undertaking (the alliance proposal) they hoped to remove suspicions.
proposed_fix: but that by postponing the proposal they hoped to strip away the suspicions

quote: The most prominent of these were Hippocrates and his brother Diomedon among the Coans, and Deinon and Polyaratus among the Rhodians.
problem: Greek breaks off mid-word: τούτων δ᾽ ἦσαν ἐπιφανέστατοι παρὰ μὲν τοῖς Κῴοις Ἱππόκριτος καὶ Διομέδων ἀδελ[...]. The text ends at ἀδελ- (presumably ἀδελφοί); the Rhodian names Deinon and Polyaratus are NOT in the Greek and are silently supplied, so the English reads as whole.
proposed_fix: The most prominent of these among the Coans were Hippocrates and Diomedon, brothers [the text breaks off here].

quote: and in the end they disappointed all expectations.
problem: Greek: καὶ πάσας ἐξήλεγχον τὰς ἐλπίδας, 'and they put every hope to the test' (they tried every resource), not 'disappointed all expectations'. The verb is ἐξελέγχω (examine, test, prove); the English reverses the sense to failure.
proposed_fix: and they put every hope to the test.

quote: Then, when he made his entrance into the senate
problem: The Greek has a gap (***) immediately before 'τότε δὲ κατὰ τὴν εἴσοδον γενόμενος τὴν εἰς τὴν σύγκλητον'; the English opens with 'Then' as if the text were continuous. The lacuna is silently smoothed.
