proposed_fix: [...] Then, when he made his entrance into the senate

quote: Because they were generally displeased by visits from kings, they issued a decree
problem: 'ὡς γὰρ καθόλου δυσαρεστούμενοι ταῖς τῶν βασιλέων ἐπιδημίαις δόγμα τι τοιοῦτον ἐξέβαλον': ὡς + participle gives the senate's alleged ground (as though displeased in general), a pretext cloaking its particular hostility to Eumenes, not a stated real cause. English turns it into a flat 'because'.
proposed_fix: On the pretext of a general displeasure at visits from kings, they issued a decree

quote: the senate dealt with all who had arrived on embassies
problem: Greek 'λοιπὸν ἡ σύγκλητος ἅπασιν τοῖς παραγεγονόσι κατὰ πρεσβείαν:' has no governing verb (colon follows directly); a verb has dropped out or the text is defective. English supplies 'dealt with' without marking it.
proposed_fix: the senate [verb missing in the Greek; sense presumably 'gave audience to'] all who had arrived on embassies

quote: taking up behavior well suited to their own theatrical excesses
problem: Greek has a lacuna: λαβόντες *** οἰκείαν ταῖς ἑαυτῶν ἀσελγείαις. The object of λαβόντες is lost; the English invents 'behavior' and reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: taking *** suited to their own excesses

quote: go beyond normal behavior, because they think that those they meet do not recognize or clearly see that they have truly been set free
problem: Greek: μείζω μὲν διαβαίνουσι τῆς κατὰ φύσιν κινήσεως, οὐ δοκοῦσι δὲ γινώσκεσθαι παρὰ τοῖς ἀπαντῶσιν οὐδὲ συνορᾶσθαι ... λέλυνται. A μὲν...δέ coordination, not causal; οὐ δοκοῦσι with passive infinitives = 'they seem not to be recognized ... nor clearly seen to have been freed'. English adds 'because' and turns the passives into 'they think'.
proposed_fix: go beyond natural movement, and seem not to be recognized by those they meet, nor clearly seen to have been set free

quote: then a chariot drawn by elephants and one drawn by a pair of horses
problem: Greek: ἐλεφάντων ἅρμα καὶ συνωρίς. Genitive ἐλεφάντων governs both: a chariot (team) of elephants and a pair (of elephants). Nothing says 'horses'.
proposed_fix: then a chariot of elephants and a pair of elephants

quote: having been compelled to wage three wars over them
problem: τριττοὺς πολέμους ἀναγκασθέντες πολεμεῖν αὐτοῖς: αὐτοῖς is dative of the peoples (the Lycians and Carians), i.e. wars waged against/with them, not wars 'over' the regions.
proposed_fix: having been compelled to fight three wars against them

quote: they sent an embassy asking the Rhodians to take them and their city into their protection
problem: The Greek reads 'πρεσβεύειν μὲν ***, ἐγχειρίζοντες σφᾶς αὐτοὺς καὶ τὴν πόλιν': there is a lacuna after πρεσβεύειν, and the Rhodians are not named in the text. The English fills the gap with an invented object and recipient.
proposed_fix: they sent an embassy [text lost in the Greek], entrusting themselves and their city

quote: But the supporters of Canuleius and Quintus testified against Menyllus and the envoys who had come from the elder brother
problem: 'τῶν δὲ περὶ τὸν Κανολήιον καὶ Κόιντον ἀπομαρτυρούντων τοῖς περὶ τὸν Μένυλλον ... διότι καὶ τὴν Κυρήνην ὁ νεώτερος καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα δι᾽ αὐτοὺς ἔχοι': Canuleius and Quintus (and their party, i.e. the commissioners themselves, not 'supporters') bore witness in support of Menyllus and the elder brother's envoys, confirming that the younger brother held Cyrene and his life through them. 'Against' inverts the sense, and the clause that follows makes sense only as corroboration.
proposed_fix: But Canuleius and Quintus and their colleagues bore witness in support of Menyllus and the envoys who had come from the elder brother

quote: seeing on the one hand that the division had been completely settled
problem: The Greek reads 'ὁρῶσα τὸν μερισμὸν *** γεγονότα τελέως': there is a lacuna between μερισμὸν and γεγονότα, and the English reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: seeing on the one hand that the division had been [text lost in the Greek] completely made

quote: pretended that he was going aboard for the voyage and slipped away
problem: The Greek is προσποιηθεὶς ὡς ἐπιναύσιος γεγονὼς ἀπηλλάττετο. ἐπιναύσιος means nauseated or sick, so Demetrius pretended to be sick (from the drinking) and left. Nothing in the Greek says he was going aboard.
proposed_fix: pretended to be sick with nausea and took his leave

quote: This was why they appointed Tiberius, because he had been an eyewitness of the whole situation.
problem: The Greek is διὸ τὸν Τεβέριον κατεστήσαντο *** πάντων αὐτόπτην γεγονέναι. The *** marks a lacuna between κατεστήσαντο and πάντων. The English reads on as if the sentence were whole, and it invents a causal 'because' clause.
proposed_fix: This was why they appointed Tiberius [text missing] to have been an eyewitness of everything.

quote: The finest quality of any letter is its power to establish goodwill.
problem: The Greek is ὅτι παντὸς ἐπιστολίου τὸ κάλλος ἐστὶ συστατικώτερον. The subject is τὸ κάλλος (beauty, or good looks) and the comparison is with παντὸς ἐπιστολίου (than any letter). So beauty is a stronger recommendation than any letter of introduction. The English inverts the sense and makes the letter the subject.
proposed_fix: Beauty is a stronger recommendation than any letter of introduction.

quote: he nevertheless left his private fortune in such a state that his family could not repay
problem: The Greek is τοσοῦτον ἀπέλειπε τὸν ἴδιον βίον ὥστε * ** μὴ δύνασθαι τὴν φερνὴν. It has a lacuna of a few words after ὥστε, before μὴ δύνασθαι. The English reads straight on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: he nevertheless left his private fortune in such a state that [text missing] his family could not repay

quote: the answer he had given to Tiberius
problem: τὴν πρὸς τὸν Τεβέριον ἀπάντησιν αὐτοῦ: ἀπάντησις here is his encounter/meeting with Tiberius, not an answer he gave.
proposed_fix: his meeting with Tiberius

quote: therefore it very nearly refused to accept them
problem: τούτους μὲν οὐ προσεδέξατο μικροῦ δεῖν: οὐ προσεδέξατο is a flat negative (the senate did not accept them, as ch. 2 states); μικροῦ δεῖν ('all but, practically') qualifies the whole statement. 'Very nearly refused' implies it did not quite refuse, i.e. it perhaps accepted them.
proposed_fix: therefore it virtually refused to accept them

quote: Envoys came from the Athenians, and from the Achaeans came Thearidas and Stephanus on behalf of the Delians.
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) after παρὰ τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἧκον πρέσβεις; the English reads on as if the sentence were whole.
proposed_fix: Envoys came from the Athenians [text missing], and from the Achaeans came Thearidas and Stephanus on behalf of the Delians.

quote: although he had three brothers close to him in age and active in affairs
problem: Greek: ἀδελφοὺς ἔχων τρεῖς καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἡλικίαν καὶ πρᾶξιν *** : there is a lacuna after πρᾶξιν (the predicate adjective(s) governing 'in age and in action' is missing). The English supplies 'close to him' and 'active in affairs' as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: although he had three brothers, [text missing] in age and in action

quote: But after summarizing his downfall, I shall bring
problem: τὴν τούτου κάθοδον: κάθοδος means 'return/going down (home)', not 'downfall'. The same word is used at the end of the paragraph for the return of Ariarathes (τὴν ἐπὶ τὰ πράγματα κάθοδον Ἀριαράθου), and ch. 12 treats Ariarathes' καταγωγή. 'Downfall' is unsupported by the Greek.
proposed_fix: But after summarizing his return, I shall bring

quote: once again sent Telecles and Anaxidamus of Megalopolis from among themselves
problem: Greek πάλιν ἐξ αὐτῆς ἔπεμπον: ἐξ αὐτῆς is the adverb 'at once, immediately'; it does not mean 'from among themselves'. The Achaeans sent Telecles and Anaxidamus again, immediately.
proposed_fix: at once sent Telecles and Anaxidamus of Megalopolis again

quote: judging from appearances alone
problem: Greek ἐκ πάντων is 'from all (indications)'; nothing in the Greek says 'alone'. The restriction to appearances alone is an addition.
proposed_fix: judging from all appearances

quote: They were to offer him five hundred talents if he would surrender Cyprus
problem: The Greek opens with a lacuna (*** προτείνειν αὐτῷ πεντακόσια τάλαντα): the governing verb and subject are lost, and προτείνειν is a dependent infinitive. The English reads as a complete sentence with an invented subject.
proposed_fix: [text lost] ... to offer him five hundred talents if he would surrender Cyprus

quote: In the years that followed, Ariarathes, after recovering the kingdom, demanded the money from them.
problem: Greek ἀπῃτοῦντο κατὰ τοὺς ἑξῆς χρόνους ὑπ᾽ Ἀριαράθου * ** , ὅτε μετέλαβε τὴν ἀρχήν: there is a lacuna after Ἀριαράθου, and ὅτε μετέλαβε τὴν ἀρχήν is a separate clause after the gap. The English joins them smoothly and hides the gap.
proposed_fix: In the years that followed they were asked for it by Ariarathes [text lost here] when he recovered the kingdom.

quote: When the senate had heard the envoys who had returned from Prusias
problem: Greek διακούσασα τῶν παρὰ τοῦ Προυσίου πρεσβευτῶν ἀνακεχωρηκότων ἐξ αὐτῆς: the envoys are Prusias' own envoys (οἱ παρὰ τοῦ Προυσίου πρεσβευταί) who had withdrawn from/left the senate, not Roman envoys returning from Prusias. ἐξ αὐτῆς may also be the adverb 'at once' going with ἀπέστειλεν, which is ambiguous.
proposed_fix: When the senate had heard the envoys sent by Prusias, who had then withdrawn

quote: Such was the course taken by events in the dispute between Attalus and Prusias.
problem: Greek ends τοιοῦτος ὅ τε κατὰ μέρος χειρισμὸς ἐγενήθη τῶν πράξεων *** : the sentence breaks off at a lacuna after ὅ τε (a corresponding clause is lost). The English closes it as if complete.
proposed_fix: Such was, on the one hand, the detailed handling of events in the dispute between Attalus and Prusias [text breaks off here].

quote: summoning prominent men to join him; and when he arrived at Ephesus
problem: Greek has a lacuna: τῶν ἐπιφανῶν ἀνδρῶν *** ἀφικόμενος δ᾽ εἰς τὴν Ἔφεσον. The English reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: summoning prominent men [text missing] and, on arriving at Ephesus

quote: since they were the legitimate offspring of King Antiochus
problem: οὖσιν Ἀντιόχου τοῦ βασιλέως ἐκγόνοις κατὰ φύσιν: 'descendants by birth/nature' (the claim is ironic in Polybius); 'legitimate' is not in the Greek (that would be κατὰ νόμον).
proposed_fix: since they were, by birth, the offspring of King Antiochus

quote: He also says that Demetrius—the man who escaped from his hostage life at Rome and became king of Syria in his thirty-third year—was a heavy drinker
problem: ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ καὶ τριακοστῇ is the book number attached to φησι (he says in the thirty-third book), not a regnal year; βασιλεύσαντα Σύρων just means 'who became king of the Syrians'.
proposed_fix: He also says in the thirty-third book that Demetrius—the man who escaped from his hostage life at Rome and became king of Syria—was a heavy drinker

quote: but also within Greece itself, you make yourself answerable
problem: The Greek has a lacuna marked * after καὶ ἐν τοῖς Ἑλληνικοῖς, before καὶ διδοῖς εὐθύνας. The English reads on as if the text were whole.
proposed_fix: but also in Greek matters [...] and you give account

quote: because he indicated the routes for sailing out through the regions of the strait
problem: τὸν προσημαίνοντα τοὺς ἔκπλους is a participle modifying Aeolus: he who gave advance signs of (foretold) the sailings out. The Greek has no causal 'because' and no word for 'routes'.
proposed_fix: who foretold the sailings out in the places along the strait

quote: from feeding on these the hunters called galeotes grow fat—fish which, he says, are also called swordfish or sea-dogs
problem: ἐκ δὲ τῆς θήρας αὐτῶν πιαίνεσθαι τοὺς γαλεώτας, οὓς καὶ ξιφίας λέγεσθαι καὶ κύνας. The galeotes are the fish that fatten from hunting the tuna's predators, not 'hunters' as men. The Greek also says both swordfish and sea-dogs (καὶ … καὶ), not 'or'.
proposed_fix: from hunting these the galeotes grow fat—fish which, he says, are called both swordfish and sea-dogs

quote: With arguments of this kind he refutes those earlier writers while claiming precision.
problem: This is the continuation of the sentence broken off in chapter 5 (ἀλλ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ἐν … οἷς ἐκείνους ἐλέγχει καθαρεύων): Polybius is not free (καθαρεύων) of such popular pronouncements even in the very matters in which he refutes the others. The English drops the negation and reverses the point, making him a careful refuter.
proposed_fix: and not even in the very matters in which he refutes those men is he free of them.

quote: ten thousand two hundred stades and more
problem: μυρίων ἐστὶ καὶ πλειόνων ἢ διακοσίων ἐπὶ τοῖς χιλίοις means 10,000 plus more than 1,200, that is, more than 11,200 stades.
proposed_fix: more than eleven thousand two hundred stades

quote: across the Sardinian Sea one may make a corresponding estimate
problem: κατὰ τὸ Σαρδόνιον δὲ λαμβάνειν συναγωγήν: across the Sardinian Sea the distance admits a contraction (is shorter). 'Corresponding' loses this, and the following ἀλλ᾽ ἔστω καὶ ἐκεῖνο τρισχιλίων ('but let that too be three thousand') is a concession for the sake of argument.
proposed_fix: across the Sardinian Sea the distance is reduced

quote: but by sea voyage it is less than five hundred.
problem: Greek: πεζῇ μὲν ... τρισχιλίων σταδίων, ... πλέοντι δὲ καὶ πεντακοσίων δέουσαν. The sea route is the 3,000 stades 'lacking five hundred', i.e. 500 stades shorter (2,500), not 'less than 500' in total.
proposed_fix: but by sea voyage it is five hundred stades shorter, that is, two thousand five hundred.

quote: Polybius in the thirty-fourth book says that Aethaleia is called Lemnos.
problem: Greek: Αἰθάλειαν τὴν Λῆμνον καλεῖσθαι. Accusative object Λῆμνον is the island being named, Αἰθάλειαν the name: Lemnos is called Aethaleia. The English reverses subject and name.
proposed_fix: Polybius in the thirty-fourth book says that Lemnos is called Aethaleia.

quote: that the seas are connected by channels because Chian and Thasian pottery is found in the Naro
problem: Greek has a gap (***) after τὸ συντετρῆσθαι τὰ πελάγη; ἀπὸ τοῦ εὑρίσκεσθαι ('from the finding of') follows the gap, so the English supplies a smooth causal link the text does not preserve.
proposed_fix: that the seas are connected by channels [gap in the Greek text] ... from the finding of Chian and Thasian pottery in the Naro

quote: Artemidorus corrects this, and not unreasonably. According to him,
problem: Greek has a gap marked after οὐκ ἀτόπως... ; the next sentence begins κατ᾽ ἐκεῖνον δὴ and English reads on as if the text were continuous.
proposed_fix: Artemidorus corrects this, and not unreasonably ... [gap in the Greek text]. According to that authority (κατ᾽ ἐκεῖνον),

quote: the poet’s words were literally true:
problem: Greek: λοιπὸν ἦν τῷ ὄντι τὸ τοῦ ποιητοῦ 'Αἴγυπτόνδ᾽ ἰέναι…' means 'what remained, in truth, was the poet's line (to go to Egypt…)'. λοιπὸν ἦν is 'there remained', not 'were true', and τῷ ὄντι is 'in truth/indeed', not 'literally'. The English turns a statement of what was left into a claim that the verse was literally true.
proposed_fix: all that remained, in truth, was the poet’s line:

quote: Though they were barbarians, they spoke at length and tried to make every point of dispute clear.
problem: Greek has a lacuna (***) after καίπερ ὄντες βάρβαροι; the English reads on as if whole and supplies 'at length'. The verb is διετίθεντο λόγους (they delivered/conducted speeches).
proposed_fix: Although they were barbarians, [text missing in the Greek] they delivered speeches and tried to make every point of dispute clear.

quote: For they were always hinting at the uncertainty of fortune
problem: Greek: τὰ τῆς τύχης ἄδηλα πολλάκις ὑπεδείκνυον, 'often', not 'always'.
proposed_fix: For they often hinted at the uncertainty of fortune

quote: who, though still young, had already been regarded as a leader in the war
problem: Greek: δοκῶν δὲ σύμβουλος γεγονέναι τοῦ πολέμου, 'thought to have been an adviser (counsellor) in respect of the war', not a leader in it.
proposed_fix: who, though still young, was thought to have been an adviser in favour of the war

quote: so Scipio fell to the ground upright and regained his footing
problem: Greek ends at ὀρθὸς ἀπέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν ὁ Σκιπίων; 'and regained his footing' is not in the Greek.
proposed_fix: so Scipio fell to the ground upright

quote: When Polybius, through Scipio, had been granted an audience on behalf of the exiles from Achaea
problem: Greek: ἐντευχθεὶς διὰ Πολύβιον ὑπὸ Σκιπίωνος. Scipio is the agent (ὑπὸ Σκιπίωνος), the approach is made on account of Polybius (διὰ Πολύβιον); nobody is 'granted an audience'. Roles of Polybius and Scipio are inverted. The grammatical subject of the participle is not given in the excerpt (opening is elliptical).
proposed_fix: When Scipio, at Polybius's instance, had made representations on behalf of the exiles from Achaea

quote: but rather to devote all their effort to discovering and recording what was truly said
problem: Greek: τὰ κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν ῥηθέντα καθ᾽ ὅσον οἷόν τε πολυπραγμονήσαντας διασαφεῖν — 'as far as possible, having investigated, to make clear what was truly said'. The qualifier καθ᾽ ὅσον οἷόν τε is dropped and replaced by an absolute 'all their effort'.
proposed_fix: but rather, as far as possible, to investigate and set out clearly what was truly said

quote: This principle having long since been firmly fixed in everyone’s mind
problem: Greek: πάλαι δὲ τούτου κεκυρωμένου βεβαίως ἐν ταῖς ἑκάστων γνώμαις — the thing long since confirmed in each man's judgment is the (lost-context) matter, i.e. the decision for war; nothing in the Greek says 'principle'. Referent of τούτου is not in the extant text, so 'principle' is invented.
proposed_fix: This (decision) having long since been firmly confirmed in the judgment of each

quote: appointed two envoys with full powers
problem: Greek: κατέστησαν πρεσβευτὰς αὐτοκράτορας, followed by five names: Γίσκων Στρυτάνος, Ἀμίλκας, Μίσδης, Γιλλίμας, Μάγων. The number is five, not two.
proposed_fix: appointed five envoys with full powers

quote: If that was not the course they chose, then they must consider once more
problem: Greek: εἰ δὲ μή, τότε πάλιν βουλεύεσθαι — 'otherwise (i.e. if the order is utterly overbearing and unexpected), then deliberate again'. The English makes the condition refer to a course of action they might not choose, misreading εἰ δὲ μή.
proposed_fix: Otherwise, they must then consider once more

quote: in the dockyard of the six-banked ships.
problem: Greek: εἰς τὸ τῆς ἑκκαιδεκήρους νεώριον *** — 'sixteen-banked' (ἑκκαιδεκήρης), singular ship, not six; and the Greek breaks off with a lacuna (***) after νεώριον, which the English reads as a complete sentence.
proposed_fix: in the dockyard of the sixteen-banked ship [...]

quote: All the senators, crying out in horror, were left as though paralyzed by the shock.
problem: Greek: οἱ δὲ πάντες ἅμ᾽ ἀνακεκραγότες ἐξ αὐτῆς οἱονεὶ παρελύθησαν — 'all of them, crying out together, were at once as if paralysed'. 'Senators' is not in the Greek (the group is unspecified in the extant text).
proposed_fix: All of them cried out together and were at once as though paralyzed.

quote: there was no more restraint
problem: Greek: οὐκέτι συνέβαινε γίνεσθαι τὴν ἀλογίαν — ἀλογία here most likely 'speechless stupor' (contrast with the preceding παρελύθησαν and the action that follows), i.e. the stupor no longer continued; 'no more restraint' reverses the sense. Meaning of ἀλογία is somewhat uncertain.
proposed_fix: the stupor no longer lasted

quote: and still others hurried toward the gates of the city
problem: Greek: οἱ δὲ πρὸς τὰς πύλας τῆς πόλεως *** — the sentence breaks off in a lacuna with no verb; the English supplies 'hurried' and reads as complete.
proposed_fix: and others [... text lost ...] to the gates of the city

quote: When men are deliberating from scratch, they should take even greater care to avoid suffering harm than to do harm to their enemies.
problem: Greek: ὁ Σκιπίων ἔφη, * ** ὅταν ἐξ ἀκεραίου βουλεύωνται, καὶ πλείω ποιεῖσθαι πρόνοιαν... — a lacuna (* **) follows ἔφη, and the speech begins mid-sentence at ὅταν; the English presents a smooth, complete quotation, inventing the main clause ('they should').
proposed_fix: [...] when they are deliberating with the matter still open, and to take more forethought not to suffer any harm than to do harm to the enemy.

quote: Scipio’s statement and his handling of the situation
problem: Greek: τῇ τοῦ Σκιπίωνος ὁμολογίᾳ καὶ τῷ χειρισμῷ τῶν πραγμάτων — ὁμολογία is 'agreement/compact' (here Scipio's arrangement, probably with Phameas), not 'statement'.
proposed_fix: Scipio’s agreement and his handling of affairs
